items.title: Latent profile analysis of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates: associations with positive acceptance and striving
items.abstract: Background The rapid integration of generative AI tools into higher education has raised concerns about problematic AI dependence and its links to academic procrastination, yet little is known about how these phenomena co-occur at the individual level among medical undergraduates. Objective This study identified latent profiles of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates, examined correlates of profile membership, and tested how profiles differ in positive acceptance and striving. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 530 undergraduates at two Chinese medical universities (March–May 2026). Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed on seven dimension sum scores from the AIDep-22 and the Academic Procrastination Scale. Multinomial logistic regression examined demographic and AI-use correlates of profile membership, and the BCH approach compared positive acceptance and striving across profiles. Results A three-profile solution best fit the data: Class 1, “low dependence–low procrastination” (41.1%); Class 2, “high dependence–high procrastination” (25.8%); and Class 3, “functional/cognitive reliance–low procrastination” (33.0%). Relative to Class 1, membership in Class 3 was associated with first-choice major enrollment (OR for non-first-choice = 0.47, 95% CI 0.30–0.75), higher subjective AI familiarity (OR for low vs. high familiarity = 0.45, 95% CI 0.27–0.74) and more frequent AI use (OR for often vs. always = 0.42, 95% CI 0.26–0.68); only AI use frequency distinguished Class 2 from Class 1 (OR for often vs. always = 0.25, 95% CI 0.15–0.42). Class 2 scored significantly lower than Classes 1 and 3 on positive acceptance and striving (all p < 0.001). Conclusions AI dependence and procrastination do not covary uniformly: a substantial subgroup exhibits elevated functional and cognitive reliance on AI without severe procrastination, while a smaller subgroup shows co-occurring dependence and procrastination together with the lowest adaptive resources. Targeted support should prioritize the latter rather than treating all frequent AI users as uniformly at risk.

items.title: Latinx Futurisms as Pedagogy
items.abstract: This chapter examines how speculative design, grounded in Latinx speculative traditions, can serve as a pedagogical framework for reimagining technological futures with and for Latinx communities. The argument unfolds through a case study of a workshop with 11 librarians serving a predominantly Latinx community in Southern California. Using restorying as a methodological approach, participants questioned dominant stereotypes that position Latinx people as disinterested or underrepresented in technology. Through engagements with generative artificial intelligence and analog collage, librarians produced two kinds of speculative work. The first involved cyborg imaginaries that fused Mexican American and Indigenous identities with technological augmentation. The second envisioned social infrastructures connecting ecological sustainability to cultural heritage and the well-being of their communities. This chapter contributes a culturally grounded approach to design education that bridges arts and sciences while affirming the cultural wealth of Latinx communities. Readers gain practical insight into how speculative workshops can be structured around restorying, alongside a theoretical framing that positions Latinx communities as creators of justice-oriented technological futures.

items.title: Law and Artificial Intelligence: The Concept of Liability and Legal Certainty under Indonesian Legal Frameworks
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across key societal sectors presents profound legal challenges, particularly regarding liability attribution and legal certainty. Operating autonomously with non-deterministic decision-making capabilities, AI deployment gives rise to risks such as copyright infringement, privacy breaches, and misinformation. Employing a normative juridical research method, this article examines whether AI can be held legally accountable under Indonesian law and evaluates the current statutory framework’s capacity to maintain legal certainty. The analysis demonstrates that Indonesian jurisprudence does not recognize AI as an independent legal subject, as it lacks moral agency and free choice. Consequently, legal responsibility remains anchored in traditional legal subjects—natural persons and corporate entities—operating in the capacity of Electronic Agents or Electronic System Providers (ESPs). Legal liability for AI-induced harm is channeled back to human developers and operating entities through established doctrines of vicarious and strict liability. Furthermore, while Indonesia currently lacks a standalone AI statute, legal certainty is preserved through an interlocking, multi-layered regulatory regime, including the Copyright Law, the Personal Data Protection Law, the Electronic Information and Transactions Law, the new Penal Code, the Government Regulation on Operation of Electronic Systems and Transactions, and the Circular Letter of the Minister of Communication and Information Technology on Artificial Intelligence Ethics. This study concludes that existing statutory frameworks provide enforceable sanctions, emphasizing that legal subjects must maintain strict compliance to mitigate technology-induced harm.

items.title: Layout-Dependent Geometry of Relational Maps: How the Same Connections Can Take Different Shapes
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Layout-Dependent Geometry of Relational Maps, a structural constraint on what a viewer can infer from a diagram of connections. Two drawings can preserve the same station order and interchanges while giving the routes different lengths, placing stations at different distances, or making different groups stand out. A diagram may therefore give a passenger reliable grounds for choosing where to change trains while giving little indication of how far apart those stations lie above ground. The paper assesses a claim drawn from a map by asking whether the coding and layout preserve the particular relation the claim concerns. Redrawing a fixed set of connections can reveal which features change with placement. Even a cluster that persists across several drawings requires an independent check of what the positions encode. A claim about how viewers interpreted the cluster requires evidence about the viewers as well. The paper places this constraint alongside Jacques Bertin’s account of visual variables in graphics and examines two transit diagrams. Harry Beck’s 1933 London Underground diagram preserved station order and interchanges while redrawing distances. In a later study using London trip data from 1998 to 2005, Zhan Guo found that passengers were more likely to choose routes that appeared shorter on the map. The 1972 New York subway diagram, produced by Massimo Vignelli’s team at Unimark with Joan Charysyn as lead designer, drew Central Park as a square. The paper examines one rider’s complaint about wayfinding, John Tauranac’s criticism of the diagram’s geography, and its replacement in 1979. Part of the Equivalence and Interchangeability series within On Human Modeling, the paper has a prospective application in human–AI interaction. An AI assistant might draw a citation network from a set of papers. Readers can check a line between two papers against their references. If the assistant also claims that papers placed close together make similar arguments, that claim requires evidence from their texts or a placement rule that explicitly encodes such similarity.

items.title: Learner-Controlled Instruction: How Does Prior Knowledge Moderate the Effect of Organizational Cues With Timeline in Video Lectures?
items.abstract: Learning scientific concepts through video lectures can be effective when visual and verbal information are presented simultaneously. The present study investigated the interaction effects of cue type (no organizational cues with timeline (NOT) vs. organizational cues with timeline (OT)) and prior knowledge (low vs. high) on learners’ attention allocation, learning performance, intrinsic motivation (i.e. interest, competence, value, and effort), and metacognition (i.e. monitoring accuracy and learning behaviors). Results indicated significant interaction effects on learning performance and monitoring accuracy. A moderated mediation analysis further revealed that OT was associated with better learning performance through more accurate monitoring among learners with high prior knowledge. Furthermore, OT efficiently directed learners’ attention to video lectures content. These findings suggest that high prior knowledge students benefit more from self-monitoring and self-regulation behaviors in learner-controlled instruction under the OT condition, whereas low prior knowledge learners may not show comparable improvement in their learning.

items.title: Learning from an innovative, live, international simulation exercise comprising a medical evacuation system for high-consequence infectious diseases: SIMEX Volare
items.abstract: Abstract Background High consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs) have high mortality rates and limited treatment options and require urgent co-ordinated public health response including sophisticated high-level isolation unit care. In the absence of a high-level isolation capacity in Ireland, the health systems of Ireland, Norway and Germany have agreed a collaborative HCID care arrangement where a patient diagnosed with a HCID in Ireland can be medically evacuated by Norwegian specialised air ambulance to Germany for ongoing care. These cross-border emergency arrangements and their coordination through EU mechanisms have not yet had to be exercised in real world circumstances. A full-scale real-time simulation exercise was devised to test pathways and use findings to improve the system. Methods This three-day, live, multi-service and cross-agency simulation tested multi-country interoperability, with over two hundred stakeholder participants. It was overseen by an international strategic exercise planning group and informed by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) simulation exercise cycle and national and ECDC guidance. Exercise evaluators assessed medical evacuation performance against predefined key performance indicators across the domains of international stakeholder activation, coordination and communication. Key Finding Such a large-scale exercise is resource-intensive, but feasible with cross-jurisdictional engagement. Intense cross-border planning was key to build relationships, clarify governance and develop harmonised guidance, pathways and procedures for testing in a safe environment. All eight high level objectives were achieved or partially achieved when measured against the pre-determined performance indicators. Findings including noting of discrepancies between different services in their high-level personal protective equipment (PPE) provision, and lack of 24-hour provision of services including laboratory diagnostics, specialised waste management, and occupational health. Lack of an agreed end-to-end transport protocol and waste-water management protocol required remedying. Following the exercise, strengthened governance and operational arrangements for preparedness and response include the development of a managed clinical network approach, enhanced operational capacity for key national services, and plans for a coordinated national HCID training and simulation programme. The findings have yielded key insights regarding interoperability across organisations and countries, and subsequent recommendations are likely to be transferable to other simulation programmes. To maintain optimal preparedness for high-stakes diseases and promote health security across Europe, partners should further incorporate international live simulation exercises to defend against cross-border health threats.

items.title: Learning how to use a Decision Support System: a simulation of Human-AI interaction frames.
items.abstract: The integration of AI in Decision Support System faces a hard limit: automation bias (Cummings, 2004). While AI may outperforms human operators in certain tasks, the added value of keeping humans-in-the-loop becomes questionable if they merely validate AI decisions. However, the ideal tool should enable complementary team performance (CTP). CTP describes a situation where the human-AI (HAI) team overcomes both AI capacity and the operator alone in terms of performance, which is incompatible with automation bias. CTP describes a one-time performance, and is not easy to achieve: it means operators stay on their mind mostly when they are correct, and change their mind mostly when the AI is correct, which is optimistic, as shown in a recent meta-analysis (Vaccaro et al., 2024).However, one observation of CTP doesn’t preclude automation bias in the long-run. Beyond a static conception of performance, the dynamics of these interactions have been studied through several theoretical perspectives (Kumar et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2023; Gonzalez et al., 2026).The stress is often put on the evolution of trust in AI through time (Chong et al., 2022), but the issue of learning effects in the task, independent of trust, is poorly understood. What is the impact of AI assistance on human skill acquisition? This question has been mostly answered in educational contexts (Fan et al., 2025; Kosmyna et al., 2025), where the delegation of cognitive tasks to the AI would hinder the learning process of the children. In operational contexts, the fear of deskilling is often expressed by experts like physicists (Natali et al., 2025), but empirical evidence is missing, to our knowledge. This gap in the literature is understandable as the inquiry is challenging: in any domain, future experts are few, their tasks to learn are numerous, and the deployment of measurement settings on long duration might be difficult.To explore this question without conducting such longitudinal studies, we propose to build a model of human learning of a technical task with an advisor. Our work develop a simulation setting on a classification task to depict possible quantitative effects of advice-taking on performance evolution through time. This modeling scheme allowed us to investigate the impact of the advisor on skill development. While most people expect that a more accurate advisor would lead the learner to higher performances, Vaccaro et al. (2024) suggest that advisors with lesser performance would be more prone to inducing CTP. This claim follows from static experimental contexts: we hereby test it in a dynamical setting. We expect that in the long-run, deskilling could happen, and would affect not-only degraded-mode performance, but also maximal running performance. Is the performance of the advisor the main factor determining performance evolution, or could the assistants have an intrinsic complementarity with the learner, depending on their classification patterns? The type of AI could lead to different results, in terms of performance, reliance, and of dependence.

items.title: Learning, leading, and innovating: Reimagining manual handling and musculoskeletal disorders as critical risks
items.abstract: Introduction Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) account for 30% of workplace harm in Aotearoa New Zealand1. Traditional manual handling training often fails because it focuses on individual behaviour rather than system design2. In 2025, Foodstuffs South Island (FSSI) challenged the status quo by giving manual handling the same priority and attention as their critical risks, noting it represented 64% of their injury claims. Moving beyond a ‘tick-box’ compliance exercise, FSSI partnered with ProErgo+ to apply a systems-thinking, ergonomics approach to risk management. Methods A 10-member Manual Handling Task Force participated in four sessions jointly facilitated by FSSI and ProErgo+. We used a structured musculoskeletal risk management framework to identify, assess, and control risks. Data was gathered through discomfort and risk factor surveys, capturing both physical and psychosocial risks. To quantify physical demands, the New Zealand Manual Handling Assessment Charts (NZMAC)3 was used for the five highest-risk tasks. Findings and proposed controls were then presented to senior leadership. Results Of the 207 workers surveyed, 75% reported discomfort. The data revealed distinct psychosocial risks between Ambient and Temperature Controlled distribution centres. The NZMAC assessments successfully pinpointed specific high-risk task elements, allowing for targeted risk reduction rather than broad, ineffective interventions. Conclusion Managing work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSDs) requires understanding the complex interactions of physical, psychosocial, environmental, organisational, and individual factors. This project succeeded by combining forward-thinking leadership with a collaborative co-design approach. By empowering workers as ‘experts’ and applying ergonomics principles, FSSI began moving from a reactive approach to proactive prevention. This model provides a transferable roadmap for any New Zealand business committed to reducing harm and improving worker wellbeing through better work design. References WorkSafe New Zealand, (2019). items.title: Lecturer Humor When AI Is at Hand: Students’ Perceptions of AI, Explanations, and Engagement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become part of how Indonesian university students learn English, yet research has focused mainly on how students use AI and not on which qualities of human teaching they still value when AI is readily available. This qualitative descriptive study explored how seventh-semester students in an Information Technology department at one vocational higher education used AI in an English course, how they compared AI-generated and lecturer explanations, and how they perceived their lecturer’s humor in relation to engagement and AI use. Open-ended online questionnaire responses from 40 students in three classes were collected in December 2025 and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis supported by frequency counts. All 40 students used AI for English learning, most often ChatGPT (31) and Gemini (21), mainly for translation, explanations, and grammar, and 13 noted limitations such as unclear or inaccurate answers. Asked whose explanations they understood better, 21 chose the lecturer, 6 chose AI, and 13 gave mixed answers. Thirty-eight students viewed the lecturer’s humor positively, associating it with a relaxed atmosphere, less boredom, enjoyment, and easier understanding, one approved of it with reservations, and one considered it a matter of personal preference. Seven contrasted the lecturer’s humor with AI, whereas two noted that AI can also joke. Students appear to value AI for flexible individual support and the lecturer’s humor for affective and relational support.

items.title: Literal or Repetitive? Exploring Lexical Diversity in Machine-generated Translations
items.abstract: Previous research has shown that machine-generated translations produced by online machine translation systems and large language models (LLMs) tend to exhibit a high degree of language standardization, notably through reduced lexical richness and limited diversity (e.g., Vanmassenhove et al. 2019, Niu 2024, Kong & Macken 2025, Yildiz Durak et al. 2025). From the perspective of creative translation, such standardization raises important questions, as lexical variety and context-sensitive reformulation are often central to translational creativity. This reduced creativity has commonly been attributed to algorithmic biases that amplify frequency effects, thereby encouraging the repeated selection of high-frequency lexical items and a preference for literal, uncreative translation strategies. Compared with human-generated translations, this reduced lexical diversity has been identified as a defining characteristic of what has been termed ‘machine-translationese’ (e.g. De Clercq et al. 2021, Vanmassenhove et al. 2021). The present study examines the extent to which online translators and LLMs favour literal English-to-French translations of lexical items with direct but less frequently used equivalents in original French, focusing specifically on 3 items: the noun thing and the verbs say and include, which are known to require non-literal translations for the sake of naturalness and idiomaticity. The online translators in this study include DeepL, Google Translate, and Reverso; the LLMs include ChatGPT-5, Gemini Flash, and Le Chat (now Vibe).The study adopts a two-stage methodology. First, a stress-test based on series of controlled English sentences was designed to elicit a range of possible French translations. The resulting outputs from the two categories of tools were analysed for literalness and lexical diversity. Results show that literal translations persist, though to a markedly lesser extent in LLMs than in online translators. While LLMs show a greater capacity for contextual adaptation, non-literal translations nonetheless remain partly repetitive and converge on a limited set of high-frequency items (e.g., the over-representation of déclarer for say). However, targeted prompting was found to both reduce literalness and encourage more diverse translation solutions, although not fully mitigating lexical standardization. Second, to test whether these tendencies persist beyond isolated sentences, the experiment was replicated on longer texts, with the compilation of a corpus of 50 English press articles (ca. 50,000 words) that were machine-translated into French using the same tools. In addition to general measures of lexical diversity in the different subcorpora (TTR, standardized TTR, Guiraud’s index, Yule’s K), normalized frequencies of the translations for the three lexical items were compared with those observed in a comparable corpus of original French press texts. Our results suggest that the main limitation lies less in literal translations than in the repeated selection of the same translation solutions, which ultimately reduces lexical diversity.Taken together, the results point to systematic forms of algorithmic bias in machine translation output. Such findings suggest that achieving natural-sounding translations that reflect actual language use still requires systematic human post-editing to reintroduce lexical diversity.The translation data for both steps was generated between the end of January and early March 2026.

items.title: Lived Experiences of Positive Solitude and AI Companion Use Among Filipino Millennials: A Phenomenological Study
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) companions has transformed how individuals experience solitude in digitally connected environments. This study explored the lived experiences of Filipino Millennials who integrate AI companions into their experiences of positive solitude. Using a qualitative phenomenological design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight Filipino Millennials who regularly engaged with AI companion platforms. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Three themes emerged: (1) Positive Solitude as an Intentional Psychological Space, (2) AI Companion as a Reflective and Emotionally Safe Presence, and (3) Balancing Autonomy and Connection in Digitally Mediated Solitude. Participants viewed positive solitude as a source of emotional recovery, self-discovery, and personal growth, while AI companions served as accessible and nonjudgmental conversational partners that supported reflection without replacing meaningful human relationships. Findings suggest that AI companions can complement positive solitude by supporting intentional AI use, emotional independence, and the maintenance of real-world social connections among Filipino Millennials.

items.title: Lived experiences of relationships to generative AI mental health chatbots among adults
items.abstract: Abstract Background Nigeria's mental health system serves less than 10% of those in need, with severe provider shortages and deep-seated stigma. Generative AI chatbots offer scalable support, yet how Nigerian adults experience attachment to non-human therapeutic agents remains unexplored. Objective To examine lived experiences of AI therapeutic relationships among Nigerian adults, focusing on attachment formation, cultural acceptability, and perceived authenticity within contexts of care scarcity. Methods Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis with 37 adults (18–45 years) who engaged AI mental health chatbots for ≥ 4 weeks. Semi-structured interviews explored relational experiences, trust development, privacy concerns, and comparisons with human/traditional healing. Results Four superordinate themes emerged: (1) Relational Ambivalence ; participants valued 24/7 availability and non-judgmental space yet struggled with perceived lack of genuine human reciprocity; (2) Cultural Navigation ; users actively adapted Western therapeutic frameworks to local idioms of distress, blending AI interactions with family counsel and spiritual practices; (3) Stigma Sanctuary ; chatbots provided confidential entry points circumventing community visibility and professional hierarchy; and (4) Fragile Dependency ; prolonged use generated attachment anxiety about potential app discontinuation or data breaches, compounded by absence of human escalation pathways. Most participants maintained "instrumental intimacy"; emotional reliance tempered by awareness of algorithmic artifice. Conclusion Nigerian adults develop pragmatic, contextually mediated attachments to AI therapeutic agents that reflect both global digital therapeutic trends and local specificities of care scarcity, stigma, and pluralistic healing. AI chatbots function not as human substitutes but as bridging objects temporary relational anchors in systems of profound unmet need. Findings suggest ethical deployment in LMICs requires culturally adaptive design, transparent algorithmic boundaries, and mandatory human handoff protocols to prevent dependency in unsupported contexts.

items.title: LLM Role Configurations in Preservice Teacher Collaborative Inquiry: Differences in AI Literacy, Cognitive Load, and Discussion Dynamics
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as conversational partners in collaborative inquiry, yet little is known about how different LLM roles are associated with preservice teachers’ learning and collaborative inquiry. This study compared four conditions: Supportive LLM that provided perspectives and information, Challenging LLM that raised counterarguments and questions, General LLM, and No-LLM. It examined differences in AI literacy, cognitive load, and discussion dynamics across these conditions. A quasi-experimental study was conducted with 210 preservice teachers who participated in online discussions on controversial issues related to AI in education. Data included self-reported AI literacy and cognitive load measures and discussion logs. Analyses included paired-samples t-tests, ANOVA, ANCOVA, content analysis, and Ordered Network Analysis. Results showed that adjusted posttest AI literacy was significantly higher in the Supportive condition than in the General LLM condition. In the General condition, AI ethics showed a significant within-condition decrease and was lower than in the Supportive condition. The General and Challenging conditions were associated with higher mental load and mental effort, whereas the Supportive condition was associated with lower levels of both. The Challenging condition showed more frequent patterns of idea integration, interpersonal exchange, and discussion facilitation. The Supportive condition showed broader exploration but fewer connections among ideas. The General condition showed repeated questioning and weaker peer idea connections. We hypothesize that the educational value of LLMs depends not only on their presence but also on how their roles are orchestrated across stages of collaborative inquiry.

items.title: LLM-Assisted Annotation for Spanish Medical Corpus Construction: An Empirical Evaluation
items.abstract: Named entity annotation in clinical text is a costly and time-intensive task, particularly for low-resource languages such as Spanish. This article introduces CLINFEM, an XML-annotated corpus comprising 1,200 Spanish medical reports from two regions of Spain. CLINFEM was created using a thorough human-in-the-loop annotation process combining large language model pre-annotation and systematic expert review. It is imperative to acknowledge that each of the 1,200 medical reports underwent meticulous review and correction by a trained human expert. Large language model pre-annotation was employed solely for the purpose of saving time and was never intended to serve as a substitute for manual annotation. Consequently, the entire CLINFEM corpus is a human-validated, gold-standard resource. GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro were evaluated as pre-annotators using a custom scheme comprising eight clinical entity types and one relational category. GPT-4o achieved a Cohen's κ of 0.73 against human annotation, while Gemini 1.5 Pro obtained κ = 0.41. Human expert review yielded an overall inter-annotator agreement of κ = 0.869 (F1 = 0.793), with a gold-standard subset agreement of κ = 0.9894. This approach reduced the overall annotation effort by around 74% compared to a fully manual approach (81% for the bulk phase alone), saving over 1,000 hours. Error rates varied by medical speciality, with oncology requiring the highest correction rate (94.3% of reports). These results demonstrate that using large language models to assist annotation is a viable and efficient strategy for constructing clinical corpora in Spanish, while also highlighting the continued necessity of human oversight.

items.title: LLMs Are Not Oracles: Knowledge Graphs Map Logical Fallacies in GenAI Math Explanations Across AI Assistants and Human Shadows
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in math education, yet little is known about how persona conditioning reshapes LLM math explanations. We examine 28,000 runs from the Math Education Digital Shadows (MEDS) dataset, spanning 14 LLMs as AI assistants (i.e., vanilla AI) or as human shadows (i.e., personifications). We analyze qualitative mathematics-related responses through textual forma mentis networks, knowledge graphs including word–word syntactic, semantic and emotional associations. We also use a DistilBERT-based classifier to flag five categories of potential logical fallacies. A regex-based check of the PCA responses showed that reassuring language was frequent but model-dependent and was not always flagged as appeal to emotion. Persona conditioning produced model-dependent changes in network size, density, and algebraic connectivity. Aggregated human-shadow responses displayed broader lexical coverage. Answers to easy and medium math questions often had no classifier-flagged fallacies, whereas an anxiety-framed PCA prompt sharply increased appeal-to-emotion and relevance labels, especially in AI-assistant mode. On an 18-item quiz, AI assistants’ accuracy exceeded human shadows’ in 10 out of 14 architectures. Expressed confidence exceeded empirical accuracy in 13 of 14 AI-assistant and 11 of 14 human-shadow conditions, a descriptive gap, not a calibration measure. These results show that (i) cognitive digital shadowing modulates LLM-generated mathematical discourse compared to the vanilla AI assistant case, and (ii) the tested LLMs are not infallible mathematics oracles. No measure here directly assesses the explanations’ mathematical validity or teaching quality.

items.title: Local Tool Failure Overextended to General Impossibility: When a Failed Instrument Is Taken for a Closed Door
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Local Tool Failure Overextended to General Impossibility, a structural constraint on what a failed attempt can establish. An instrument may lack an operation that a task requires. When someone takes that limit as grounds for declaring the task impossible under any arrangement, a claim about the instrument becomes a claim about the activity itself. The paper assesses such a claim by asking where the barrier lies. A feature of the world, a governing rule, missing information, or the design of the instrument can each prevent an attempt from succeeding. Success with a different instrument establishes that the activity is possible under that arrangement. Explaining the original failure requires identifying what changed between attempts. The paper places this question alongside Steven Maier and Martin Seligman’s work on learned helplessness and asks what evidence warrants carrying a judgment of futility from one setting into another. A 1911 newspaper article reasoned from the number of Chinese characters that no typewriter could be large enough to print the language. Its conclusion rested on a design assumption: each character would need its own key. By 1947, tray and drum machines already let operators select Chinese characters. Lin Yutang’s MingKwai prototype offered a keyboard solution in which the typist entered character components and selected from the candidates displayed in a window. The 1890 U.S. census supplies a contrast. Faced with the time hand tabulation would require, officials held a competition for a better method and adopted Herman Hollerith’s punched-card system. Part of the Inquiry and Possibility series within On Human Modeling, the paper has a potential application in human–AI evaluation. An assistant may search a scanned register for a name, find no match, and report that the entry cannot be recovered. An archivist who finds the name on the same page image establishes that recovery was possible. Checking whether the scan contained a searchable text layer can then explain why the assistant’s particular method failed.

items.title: LogReasoner: Empowering LLMs with Expert-Like Coarse-to-Fine Reasoning for Automated Log Analysis
items.abstract: Log analysis is crucial for monitoring system health and diagnosing failures in complex systems. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for automated log analysis, leveraging their reasoning capabilities to perform tasks such as anomaly detection and failure prediction. However, general-purpose LLMs struggle to formulate structured reasoning workflows that align with expert cognition and deliver precise details of reasoning steps. To address these challenges, we propose LogReasoner, a coarse-to-fine reasoning enhancement framework designed to enable LLMs to reason log analysis tasks like experts. LogReasoner consists of two stages: (1) coarse-grained enhancement of expert thinking, where high-level expert thoughts are constructed from collected troubleshooting flowcharts and existing tasks to enable LLMs to formulate structured reasoning workflows and (2) fine-grained enhancement of specific steps, where we first fine-tune the LLM with task-specific stepwise solutions to enhance the LLM for instantiated reasoning, then employ the preference learning to calibrate the LLM’s reasoning details from its mistakes, further strengthen the LLM’s analytical granularity and correctness. We evaluate LogReasoner on four distinct log analysis tasks using open source LLMs such as Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3. Experimental results show that LogReasoner significantly outperforms existing LLMs, achieving state-of-the-art performance and demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs for log analysis. Our source code and detailed experimental data are available at https://github.com/LeaperOvO/LogReasoner .

items.title: Longitudinal fall patterns in Parkinson’s disease: automated narrative extraction in 2811 patients
items.abstract: Abstract Fall vulnerability in Parkinson’s disease (PD) evolves through the longitudinal accumulation of motor and nonmotor features routinely documented in clinical narratives but inaccessible to structured electronic health record analysis at scale. We created a reusable platform for PD outcomes research using a few-shot large language model-based pipeline capable of extracting fall occurrence, recent fall frequency, and nine prespecified risk-modifying domains from outpatient neurology documentation. The pipeline was validated against expert consensus in 2557 notes and applied to 25,758 notes from 2811 patients at a tertiary movement disorders center (2012–2025). Final-model agreement closely approximated expert interrater agreement for fall occurrence (κ = 0.841 vs 0.891) and recent fall frequency (κ = 0.889 vs 0.892), while several risk-modifying domains achieved agreement comparable to or exceeding human annotators. We then used lagged generalized estimating equation models to test whether NLP-derived fall status and risk-modifying domains predicted fall occurrence at the subsequent visit. A prior fall (OR, 3.23; 95% CI, 2.89–3.61), motor progression (OR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.11–1.34), and motor complications (OR, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.03–1.23) independently predicted next-visit falls. This study establishes a scalable framework for narrative phenotyping of PD fall vulnerability.

items.title: Machine Governance Beyond Man vs. Machine: Toward a Theory of Situated Machine Knowing, Machine-Operational Policy, Control, and Justified Agency
items.abstract: Governance of artificial intelligence is usually narrated as a contest over control between people and machines. This paper develops a governance theory that does not begin from that premise. It asks instead under what conditions a machine is justified in treating a state as known, and under what conditions it is entitled to act on it. We propose four machine-operational constructs. A knowledge property graph (KPG) holds the authority a machine acts under, each claim quoted from the authority's text or attested by a named person. A machine KPG (mKPG) holds what the machine is justified in treating as known about one situation at one time, each assertion bound to the instrument through which it entered. mPolicy is a machine-operational realization of policy, mControl a mechanism that governs machine knowing and acting under it, and mGovernance the governance that results. The normative tier is not only proposed: for the KPG, prior work proves that a committed decision is the authority's decision under premises its witness names, and locates the failed premise when a commitment is wrong. We state eight falsifiable propositions, set them against published evidence that bears on five of them, give a pre-registration-ready design for the proposition on which the epistemic tier rests, and compare the architecture with adjacent frameworks. The paper reports no new experiments. Its contribution is the theory, the formal grounding of its normative tier, an account of what existing evidence already shows, and a program for testing the rest.

items.title: Machine learning-driven regulation of the four-electron LiOH pathway in lithium–oxygen batteries with prolonged cycling
items.abstract: Abstract The practical deployment of high-energy-density lithium–oxygen batteries is fundamentally restricted by sluggish oxygen redox kinetics and the instability of discharge intermediates. Here, we report an artificial intelligence-integrated framework leveraging interpretable machine learning and density functional theory to navigate a vast chemical space of thousands of active sites. This approach identifies Ni-Co dual-atom catalysts as a better configuration among the selected elements for orchestrating multi-electron transfer. Theoretical analysis reveals that synergistic electronic coupling between the dual-sites fundamentally reconfigures the d -band center, thereby lowering the thermodynamic barriers for oxygen redox. Moreover, the catalysts enable precise regulation of the reaction pathway, inducing a controllable transition from the conventional two-electron pathway to a four-electron pathway. This shift yields a discharge capacity of ~60,000 mAh g −1 . Beyond its role as a positive electrode catalyst, this architecture functions as a multifunctional interfacial protective layer that stabilizes the lithium metal negative electrode by suppressing dendrite growth. Consequently, the lithium–oxygen system achieves stable lifespan of 2075 cycles under the four-electron pathway with reduced voltage decay. This work establishes a data-guided strategy for the rational design of atomic-scale architecture via artificial intelligence, unlocking the potential of multi-electron oxygen chemistry for lithium–oxygen batteries.

items.title: Machine learning–based surveillance and forecasting of infectious diseases: a systematic review of modeling approaches and multi-source data integration
items.abstract: Abstract Background Enteric infections, including rotavirus gastroenteritis, place a heavy burden on children and low-resource health systems. Surveillance still depends on laboratory-confirmed case reporting that moves slowly through hospital information systems (HIS), electronic medical records (EMR), and laboratory information systems (LIS), offering little predictive lead time. Digital health infrastructure and artificial intelligence (AI) now offer a way to rebuild surveillance around combined, near-real-time data. Methods Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020, we searched PubMed and IEEE Xplore (through July 2026, with a supplementary PubMed search in September 2026) for studies using statistical, machine learning, deep learning, or multi-source AI-driven methods for infectious disease surveillance or forecasting, with attention to enteric infections and methodologically transferable work. Additional studies were identified through reference citation searching. Two reviewers screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias (PROBAST for 23 prediction-model studies; narrative appraisal for 5 ecological association studies; contextual studies were not formally appraised). Results Thirty-three studies were included: 28 formal studies — statistical models ( n = 5), machine learning approaches ( n = 8), deep learning approaches ( n = 4), and multi-source digital surveillance ( n = 11) — and five contextual studies (environmental monitoring, virus–host association, simulation, surveillance-signal, and network studies) analyzed separately. Data sources broadened over time from meteorological and clinical records to EMR, telehealth, wastewater, internet-search, social-media, water-quality, and genomic streams. Machine learning and deep learning approaches were increasingly applied alongside conventional methods to model nonlinear and lagged exposure–response patterns and to integrate heterogeneous data streams, and multi-source systems—including wastewater-based and syndromic designs—reported earlier signal detection than single-source designs. Most evidence, however, is retrospective in design—spanning single-site to national and multinational datasets—and external validation and prospective deployment were largely absent. Conclusions The reviewed evidence suggests that AI-supported approaches may improve infectious disease surveillance by enabling earlier detection of epidemiological changes and supporting more timely public health responses. Operational use will depend less on retrospective accuracy than on external validation, interpretability, and integration with existing surveillance infrastructure.

items.title: Making learning visible in the age of generative AI: reported assessment practices for cognitive engagement and self-regulated learning, and the development and external appraisal of a higher education assessment framework
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.

items.title: Mapping artificial intelligence for science with open metadata reveals shifting evidence regimes across scientific domains
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) is often discussed as a unified transformation, although scientific domains differ markedly in how model outputs are tested, validated, and justified. We map an audited corpus of N=2,784 records (2014–2025) retrieved from Crossref and screened with a frozen, versioned rulebook, and compare evidence regimes in protein science, materials design, drug discovery, closed-loop experimentation, and mathematical reasoning. Using term co-occurrence, reference co-citation, burst detection, growth models, and collaboration networks, we identify three robust patterns: (i) rapid but decelerating growth (Poisson rate 1.381, 95% CI 1.361–1.402, declining from 1.537 in 2014–2019 to 1.320 in 2019–2025); (ii) a coherent term-co-occurrence structure (75 nodes, modularity Q=0.404 ) organized around four measured streams—representation learning, generative and inverse design, closed-loop experimentation, and neuro-symbolic reasoning—with the generative stream acting as the connecting hub; and (iii) a right-boundary rise in large language model terminology (burst state 3) that a year-by-year backtest shows is not a last-observation artefact. The maps are sensitive to metadata availability: abstract coverage is 50.6%, reference coverage 84.3%, and a title-only variant changes the network partition substantially (adjusted Rand index 0.762), so the maps describe the screened open-metadata corpus rather than the total AI4S literature. Cross-domain analysis shows that AI most consequentially shifts scientific bottlenecks from representation and candidate generation toward experimental or formal validation, provenance, and responsibility for claims. We contribute an auditable, open-metadata science-mapping workflow designed for reproducibility and an evidence-regime framework for analysing how epistemic labour is redistributed across models, instruments, formal verifiers, infrastructures, and human experts.

items.title: Mathematics Teacher Interaction Styles with Generative Artificial Intelligence: Personalization in Word- Problem Design
items.abstract: Abstract As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) plays an increasing role in K-12 mathematics classrooms, understanding how teachers collaborate with these technologies during instructional design is essential. Drawing on frameworks related to personalization theory, Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge, and adaptive epistemic agency, this study examined how seven seventh-grade mathematics teachers interacted with ChatGPT to personalize mathematics word problems to students’ interests. Analyses of teacher-GenAI interactions identified three interaction styles: AI-Dominated-Passive Prompt Personalization, Teacher-Dominated-Rigid Personalization, and Human-AI partnership-Collaborative Personalization. Students' ratings of the resulting personalized problems varied across teachers and interaction styles, with the strongest positive patterns occurring among teachers characterized by Collaborative Personalization. Collaborative personalization illustrates how teachers may maintain epistemic authority for evaluating mathematical, pedagogical, and contextual appropriateness while selectively granting GenAI generative authority to expand personalization possibilities. These findings highlight the importance of preparing teachers to critically evaluate and collaboratively engage with GenAI during instructional design.

items.title: Mechanomedicine for Lung Transplantation: From Multiscale Forces to AI‐Assisted Translation
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Long‐term outcomes after lung transplantation remain limited by primary graft dysfunction and chronic lung allograft dysfunction, despite improvements in surgery, immunosuppression and infection control. Mechanical injury is a complementary contributor that remains insufficiently integrated into transplant care. The lung allograft must accommodate cyclic ventilation, reperfusion shear, thoracic constraints and matrix remodeling. These forces can disrupt the alveolar‐capillary barrier, amplify inflammation and activate fibrotic programmes. Here we synthesize lung transplantation through a mechanomedicine framework that links organ‐scale loading, cellular mechanotransduction and clinical decision‐making. We discuss how computational models and artificial intelligence (AI) can integrate ex vivo lung perfusion waveforms, imaging‐derived ventilation or strain patterns, and molecular injury markers to support graft‐risk assessment. We then organize mechanotherapeutic strategies by clinical readiness, from protective ventilation, size matching and extracorporeal graft support to emerging interventions targeting mechanotransduction according to cell type and loading conditions. Finally, we outline a translational roadmap for standardized mechanical biomarkers, interpretable AI and clinician‐supervised digital‐twin models.

items.title: MedFlow: Investigating the Accessibility of a Dual-Path AI-Assisted Appointment Registration Interface for Older Adults in Healthcare
items.abstract: Navigating complex digital healthcare interfaces imposed a disproportionate cognitive burden on older adults, particularly when fragmented workflows in outpatient appointment registration undermined independent access and necessitated family assistance. To address this, we developed MedFlow, a structured AI-assisted registration system that augments a linear baseline interface with a non-linear AI support layer that offers natural-language input, contextual recommendations, and real-time guidance. In a mixed-methods study with 22 older adults, we compared MedFlow against a traditional mobile registration system. Results showed that MedFlow significantly outperformed the traditional system across all dimensions. The AI-assisted approach notably improved task efficiency and technology acceptance. Moreover, both self-reported and multi-modal physiological data triangulated to confirm substantially improved cognitive performance. Participants also reported superior pragmatic and hedonic qualities, alongside increased feelings of competence and enjoyment. This study highlighted the potential of hybrid AI-assisted healthcare structures to mitigate cognitive barriers and support older adults’ autonomy.

items.title: MENTORA: AN INTELLIGENT AI-DRIVEN FRAMEWORK FOR ACADEMIC WORKFLOW AUTOMATION AND OUTCOME-BASED EDUCATION MANAGEMENT
items.abstract: This paper presents MENTORA, an intelligent AI-driven framework designed to automate and centralize faculty-oriented academic workflows in higher education institutions. The proposed platform integrates academic planning, syllabus progress tracking, timetable management, student roster management, attendance monitoring, assessment preparation, course outcome mapping, and faculty assistance within a unified application. MENTORA is developed using Python, Flask, Flask-Login, Flask-SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Bootstrap. It incorporates Google's Gemini models for multimodal timetable and student roster information extraction, as well as AI-assisted faculty support and assessment content generation. Scikit-learn is used for question classification based on Bloom's taxonomy and difficulty levels, while TF-IDF similarity supports course outcome mapping and duplicate question detection. The framework follows a hybrid AI architecture that combines generative AI, conventional machine learning, text similarity analysis, and rule-based processing while retaining faculty oversight for important academic decisions. This paper describes the problem context, related work, objectives, system architecture, functional modules, implementation technologies, workflow design, security considerations, and a proposed evaluation methodology. Quantitative performance results and expert validation are not reported in this manuscript; these remain subjects for future empirical evaluation. Keywords: Academic workflow automation, Artificial Intelligence, Generative AI, Higher Education, Machine Learning, Bloom's Taxonomy, Outcome-Based Education.

By combining quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) modeling, physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations, and multi-omics analysis, AI-driven systems enable mechanistic understanding of nano–bio interactions. Approaches such as nano-QSAR, read-across modeling, and systems toxicology improve hazard identification and support safer-by-design strategies. Integration of deep learning with dosimetry and metabolic network modeling enhances predictive performance across exposure routes, thereby accelerating risk assessment and regulatory decision-making in nanotoxicology.

items.title: Modelo pedagógico mediado por inteligencia artificial generativa para promover el pensamiento crítico y el aprendizaje significativo en educación media colombiana
items.abstract: La incorporación de inteligencia artificial generativa en la educación media plantea una tensión entre su potencial de apoyo y el riesgo de sustituir procesos cognitivos esenciales. El objetivo de este estudio fue diseñar un modelo pedagógico mediado por inteligencia artificial generativa que promueva pensamiento crítico y aprendizaje significativo en estudiantes de educación media colombiana, bajo una perspectiva humanocéntrica de Sociedad 5.0. Se desarrolló una investigación cualitativa, documental, interpretativa y teórico-propositiva. El corpus estuvo compuesto por 40 fuentes: 35 sustantivas y cinco metodológicas, examinadas mediante ocho categorías y una ruta de diez fases. La síntesis produjo ocho hallazgos documentales y sustentó CRISOL-IA 5.0, integrado por diez principios, siete componentes y seis fases: Contextualizar, Recuperar, Interrogar, Someter a contraste, Organizar y Lograr transferencia. Su funcionamiento se representó en una secuencia demostrativa de cuatro sesiones para grado décimo, con seis evidencias observables. La comprobación conceptual mostró cobertura de las seis fases y los siete componentes; de nueve criterios funcionales, seis se cumplieron en el diseño, dos quedaron condicionados por el contexto institucional y uno —eficacia educativa— requiere aplicación con participantes. Se concluye que el aporte ofrece una arquitectura pedagógica trazable y adaptable, sin constituir todavía una validación empírica.

items.title: Modern Digital Tools for Monitoring the Implementation of Strategic Program Documents of the Russian Federation
items.abstract: The article examines digital monitoring of the implementation of strategic program documents of the Russian Federation and its connection to the evaluation of political and administrative decisions. It aims to identify the functions of modern information tools and the conditions for the managerial suitability of the data they gener-ate. The methods employed include normative analysis, functional comparison of government information systems, and qualitative document analysis. The research materials comprise legal acts, official publications of the Federal Treasury, and scholarly papers on public administration. Monitoring practices described in 2024 are compared with institutional changes introduced in 2026. The article identifies the distribution of functions be-tween the State Automated System “Upravlenie”, the State Integrated Information System “Electronic Budget”, and the state statistical platform within the unified plan for achieving national goals. It establishes the im-portance of accounting for the relationships between activities, indicators and national goal components, pre-serving the revision history, and documenting corrective action. The article proposes an analytical monitoring record, along with six criteria for the managerial suitability of monitoring, covering goal alignment, evidential support, temporal comparability, revision history, cross-system comparability, and completeness of response. The article also explores the conditions for verifying relationships and predictive signals derived with the use of artificial intelligence. The paper concludes that digital tools should be studied together with procedures for building evidence and using information within the competences of management participants.

items.title: Multiple disease detection and prediction using advanced computing technologies: a comprehensive systematic review
items.abstract: Multimorbidity—the concurrent presence of two or more chronic long-term conditions—affects more than 37% of the global adult population and consumes 55%–80% of healthcare expenditure in high-income systems, yet artificial intelligence (AI) diagnostic systems remain overwhelmingly disease-specific, creating a profound structural mismatch with the multi-disease complexity characterizing the majority of real-world clinical encounters across twelve review-defined disease groups mapped to World Health Organization (WHO) ICD-11 chapters. This systematic review, following PRISMA 2020 and registered with OSF.IO (Registration DOI number: 10.17605/OSF.IO/3HZ45; Date of Registration: 25 October 2026), evaluated advanced AI technologies for simultaneous multi-domain disease detection and prediction. Nine electronic databases, PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Springer Link, Wiley, MDPI, and Google Scholar, were searched for peer-reviewed literature published from January 2015 to 31 August 2026. Database-specific Boolean searches (full strings in Supplementary Table S1 ) combined AI terms with terms for the twelve review-defined disease groups. Quality appraisal was done using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST tools (Cohen's κ = 0.84 refers to study screening agreement). Of 4,215 records identified (3,368 after removing 847 duplicates; 612 full texts assessed; 332 excluded), 280 studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 185 provided quantitative performance data for a descriptive (non-pooled) synthesis. Deep learning models such as CNN, LSTM, ViT, and GNN reported high but heterogeneous discrimination across the twelve disease groups (AUC: 0.85–0.991). These values come from different tasks, datasets, and validation designs; they are not pooled estimates and do not show superiority of any architecture. Three of the highest-reporting single-disease studies (retrospective and not directly comparable) include: diabetic retinopathy detection (AUC 0.991; n = 128,175); cancer whole-slide image classification (AUC 0.98; n = 44,732); and cardiac arrhythmia detection (AUC 0.97; n = 91,232 ECGs). Convolutional neural networks were the most popular network type (26% of studies), while the main programming language was Python (68%). Three repeated gaps can be seen in the field of research in general, and those are: 1) lack of representation of people from developing countries in the training data; 2) scarce evidence from randomized prospective trials showing improved patient outcomes; and 3) an underdeveloped regulatory pathway for multi-disease AI as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). Realizing simultaneous multi-disease AI at clinical scale demands five coordinated priorities: standardized cross-category benchmarks, demographically inclusive datasets with mandatory low- and middle-income country representation, prospective randomized trial validation, federated privacy-enhancing infrastructure designed to support GDPR, HIPAA, and DPDPA 2023 compliance (federated learning alone does not establish compliance), and internationally harmonized regulatory governance for multi-disease Software as a Medical Device authorization. Limitations of the review itself (English-only restriction, heterogeneity, overlapping public datasets, publication bias) are discussed in Section 8.5 . items.title: Narrative Threat Zine-ing: Storytelling and Reproductive Privacy Communication
items.abstract: The U.S. reproductive health landscape is fragmented, with legal, digital, and interpersonal privacy risks that are highly contextual and often poorly addressed by conventional privacy guidance. Prior work has proposed narrative threat modeling as an alternative to predominantly technical approaches to reproductive privacy communication. Building on this work, we introduce narrative threat zine-ing , a qualitative method that invites participants to communicate reproductive privacy through story and form rather than checklists or technical instruction. We report findings from four zine-making workshops in which participants created zines for people they worried about in the post- Roe landscape. Participants consistently framed reproductive privacy through relationships, lived experience, and storytelling, positioning zines as tools for awareness, solidarity, and collective sensemaking rather than prescriptive guidance. We argue that narrative threat zine-ing offers a method for examining how people interpret and communicate reproductive privacy under conditions of legal and social uncertainty.

items.title: NatBDI: Combining BDI reasoning and natural language inference for autonomous agents
items.abstract: Abstract Developing autonomous agents to deal with real-world problems is challenging, especially when developers are not necessarily specialists in artificial intelligence. Recent advances in machine learning for natural language processing tasks are reaching performance levels suitable for practical applications, although these approaches rely on opaque, inscrutable models. This poses three key challenges: the interface between the programming and the developer, the efficiency of the resulting agents, and the scrutiny of their behaviour. We tackle the challenge of developing autonomous agents over natural language environments in an efficient agent architecture that leverages recent developments in natural language processing and the intuitive folk psychology abstraction of the beliefs, desires, intentions (BDI) architecture. This paper introduces NatBDI , a new class of agent architecture that uses the BDI reasoning cycle with components driven by natural language processing. This allows a developer to instruct the agent more directly using a combination of controlled natural language structure and natural language knowledge as its programming interface. The resulting architecture handles natural language environments using a combination of language models and natural language inference to bootstrap the agent’s reasoning. We empirically assess the efficiency gains of this combination while introducing a more intuitively programmed autonomous agent. Instructions in this interface substantially improve agent performance in the experimental scenario over a baseline agent created using a pure machine learning approach. The resulting architecture shows that combining learned policies with intuitively engineered domain knowledge yields substantial performance gains. We expect this class of agents to provide a powerful, yet intuitive, tool for agent-driven programming.

items.title: Navigating the Sea of Reviews: Unveiling the Effects of Introducing AI-Generated Summaries in E-Commerce
items.abstract: AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. items.title: Negotiating Control and Accountability among Stakeholders in High-Risk AI Use Cases: Development and Evaluation of the Method ALIGN
items.abstract: Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate AI risks. We describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN and discuss how this method promotes AI governance by highlighting the relevance of control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle.

items.title: Nipple-Sparing Mastectomy in BRCA1/2 Carriers: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Breast Cancer Occurrence After Risk-Reducing and Therapeutic Procedures
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Nipple-sparing mastectomy (NSM) is increasingly performed in BRCA1/2 carriers, both for risk reduction and for treatment of breast cancer, but concern remains about glandular tissue left beneath the preserved nipple. We summarised the oncological outcomes of NSM in carriers. Methods: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PubMed Central (Europe PMC) up to 30 September 2026, CENTRAL on 26 September 2026, and Embase on 7 November 2026 and screened the citations of relevant articles for series reporting outcomes of NSM in BRCA1/2 carriers. The outcomes were breast cancer diagnosed after risk-reducing NSM and locoregional recurrence after therapeutic NSM; cancers found at surgery were not counted. Proportions per woman were pooled with a binomial random-effects model (generalised linear mixed model, no continuity correction) and are reported as marginal (average-risk) and median-type (typical-study) proportions, with crude proportions, a beta-binomial model, follow-up strata, and approximate person-time analyses as checks. Two human reviewers went through all articles, with generative AI used only as an assistant, and the statistics were reviewed by a third author. Risk of bias was assessed with an adapted Joanna Briggs Institute checklist and certainty of evidence with GRADE. Results: Fifteen studies were included. After risk-reducing NSM, seven breast cancers occurred among 1215 women from eleven studies (crude proportion 0.58% (exact 95% CI 0.23–1.18%); model-based marginal proportion 0.60%, median-type 0.41% (95% CI 0.04–1.07%)); follow-up ranged from 33 to 129 months, and four of the seven cancers came from one international registry. After therapeutic NSM, locoregional recurrence occurred in 16 of 363 women from five studies (crude 4.4% (exact 95% CI 2.5–7.1%); model-based marginal proportion 4.3%, median-type 4.2% (95% CI 1.1–6.9%)); one study contributed 11 of the 16 events. Recurrence within the nipple–areolar complex was reported explicitly by only one study (none in 114 breasts). Sensitivity analyses yielded median-type proportions of 0.30% to 0.74% after risk-reducing NSM and 2.6% to 4.2% after therapeutic NSM. Risk of bias was moderate to high in most studies, and the certainty of the evidence was very low for both outcomes. Conclusions: In BRCA1/2 carriers, about 0.6% of women had breast cancer after risk-reducing NSM and about 4% had locoregional recurrence after therapeutic NSM, but follow-up was short and heterogeneous and the certainty of the evidence is very low. These data describe observed event frequencies and do not establish oncological safety or equivalence to other mastectomy techniques; longer prospective studies with time-to-event, gene-specific, and comparative reporting are needed.

items.title: O uso de Languaging nas aulas de Português como Língua de Herança
items.abstract: This study aims to discuss and analyze the use of Languaging as a tool for linguistic construction in the teaching and learning process of Portuguese as a Heritage Language. The Languaging process is examined through Language-Related Episodes (LREs), understood as analytical tools for investigating learners’ linguistic reflection and for supporting pedagogical practices in heritage language education, more specifically in Portuguese. The study is based on the analysis of interactions that occurred in a Portuguese as a Heritage Language classroom context with participants living in South Africa, aged between 10 and 11. The main findings indicate that the LREs identified in the study are predominantly related to grammatical aspects and structural mechanisms of writing, and they highlight the crucial role of teacher mediation in learners’ cognitive engagement. The conclusions suggest that the use of Languaging in collaborative writing activities constitutes a powerful analytical and pedagogical tool for Portuguese as a Heritage Language instruction, as it promotes the articulation between form, meaning, and discourse, fostering interculturality in the classroom, while also underscoring the need for teacher education specifically focused on heritage language instruction and sensitive to the linguistic and sociocultural particularities of heritage speakers.

items.title: Occupation-Specific Associations Between Psychosocial Stress and Low Back Pain Among Healthcare Workers: Evidence from Japan’s Mandatory Stress Check Program
items.abstract: Abstract Low back pain (LBP) is a common occupational health problem among healthcare workers. While physical demands are known to contribute to LBP, few large-scale studies have investigated the contribution of psychosocial stressors. This study examined the association between occupational LBP and stress-related factors at a university hospital in Japan. In this cross-sectional study, we analyzed responses to the Brief Job Stress Questionnaire administered to 2,450 staff members. Participants were categorized into LBP and non-LBP groups. The prevalence of LBP and high stress was compared by occupation. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with LBP. The overall prevalence of frequent LBP was 29.1%, being highest in nurses (39.3%) and lowest in doctors (11.1%). The odds ratio for LBP in nurses versus doctors was 3.54 (95% confidence interval 2.22–5.63). High stress status was more common in the LBP group than in the non-LBP group (25.1% versus 6.9%). Multivariate analysis showed that subjective physical workload, interpersonal stress in the workplace, physical fatigue, depressive symptoms, support from supervisors, work/life satisfaction, and body mass index were independently associated with LBP. These findings provide epidemiological evidence that both physical and psychosocial stressors are associated with occupational LBP among healthcare workers.

items.title: Occupational Hazards and Safety Practices Among Brewery Workers in Rivers State, Nigeria
items.abstract: The study focused on the occupational hazards and safety practices among brewery workers in Rivers State. Six specific objectives, research questions and 6 hypotheses were raised and tested at a 0.05 level of significance. The research design adopted for the study was a descriptive survey design using triangulation mixed method. The population of the study was one thousand six hundred (1,600) workers in brewery industry in Rivers state. The sample size for the study was 671 workers and 8 participants for the qualitative study; the sample size was determined using fishers formula for calculating sample size. The instrument for data collection was a structured questionnaire and unstructured interview guide for the qualitative study; a reliability coefficient of 0.84 was obtained. The result showed that workers exposure to physical, biological, ergonomic, mechanical, chemical and psychosocial hazards were low, findings revealed that the grand mean of 2.65 ± 0.34 indicated a high extent of safety practices among brewery workers. The result illustrated a correlation coefficient, r = -0.05 indicating a very low relationship between hazards exposure and safety practices. It was recommended among others that Management of brewery companies should immediately institute and implement safety measures to avoid occupational risks and put in place adequate preparedness against other hazards, Management of brewery companies should always organize workshop aiming at promoting occupational safety and health through appropriate prevention programs and provision of comprehensive occupational health and safety services with the provisions of personal protective devices, and focused interventions for workers.

items.title: Occupational health and safety as a link between environmental safety and production efficiency: a moderated mediation analysis
items.abstract: Background Maintaining safe workplace environments in manufacturing industries is important for ensuring employees' health and maintaining effective production performance. Research on environmental safety and occupational health and safety is extensive, but the association between environmental safety and production efficiency and whether employees' safety knowledge supports this relationship, has received limited attention. Methods Data were collected from two independent cross-sectional purposive samples of footwear production workers (Wave 1 and Wave 2; N = 385 each), 3 months apart, and analyzed separately using Hayes PROCESS macro model 7 to investigate the indirect association between environmental safety and production efficiency through occupational health and safety, and the moderating effect of safety knowledge, with a simple slope test used to probe the interaction. Total effects were estimated using model 4. Results Contrary to the hypothesized direction, the association between environmental safety and occupational health and safety was weaker at higher safety knowledge in both waves; the interaction was significant after correction for multiple testing in Wave 1 only. In Wave 1, the interaction was a crossover: environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety only at low safety knowledge, and the indirect effect on production efficiency was significant only at low safety knowledge. The direct and total effects were not significant. In Wave 2, environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety at all levels of safety knowledge, with the association weakening as knowledge increased. The indirect effect was significant at low, mean and high safety knowledge, and the direct and total effects were also significant, indicating partial mediation. Conclusion In both waves, environmental safety was indirectly associated with production efficiency through occupational health and safety, at least among workers with lower safety knowledge, and this indirect association was weaker among workers with higher safety knowledge. These cross-sectional findings suggest that safe working environments may be particularly relevant for workers with lower safety knowledge.
