items.title: Occupational Health and Safety Knowledge and Perceived Impact of Health Education Among Municipal Waste Workers in Calabar, Nigeria: An Exploratory Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Municipal solid waste workers operate in high-risk environments with limited institutional support, exposing them to diverse occupational hazards. This study explored occupational health and safety knowledge, practices, and experiences among municipal waste workers in Calabar, Nigeria, and examined the perceived impact of a health education intervention using a qualitative approach. A qualitative exploratory design was employed, involving Key Informant Interviews (KII) with 12 managers and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) with 36 waste workers. Data were collected using semi-structured interview guides and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings revealed low baseline knowledge of occupational hazards, poor safety practices, and systemic barriers such as inadequate provision of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), weak monitoring, funding constraints, and poor prioritization of worker health. The intervention improved awareness and perceived understanding of occupational hazards and safety practices, although structural barriers persisted. The study concludes that health education enhances knowledge but must be complemented by systemic reforms, including provision of PPE, enforcement of safety policies, and improved worker welfare.

items.title: Occupational health and safety knowledge varies by settlement duration, residency status, and previous training among construction workers in Ontario, Canada
items.abstract: Introduction Occupational health and safety (OHS) knowledge is important for identifying worker training needs and informing workplace injury prevention strategies. However, immigrant workers are often treated as a homogeneous group despite differences in settlement duration, residency status, and previous training experiences that may influence their knowledge of workplace rights, responsibilities, and safe work practices. This exploratory study examined differences in OHS knowledge among immigrants residing in Ontario for >5 years, immigrants residing in Ontario for ≤5 years, and Canadian-born construction workers in Ontario, Canada. Methods A cross-sectional survey of 206 construction workers assessed OHS knowledge using scenario-based questions developed with reference to Ontario OHS requirements. Associations between OHS knowledge scores and participant characteristics were examined using univariable analyses and a generalized linear model. Results Immigrants residing in Ontario for >5 years had higher OHS knowledge scores than immigrants residing in Ontario for ≤5 years. Knowledge also differed by residency status, with Canadian citizens born outside Canada and permanent residents scoring higher than Canadian-born and temporary-resident participants. In the adjusted model, longer residence in Ontario, residency status, and previous OHS training outside Ontario were significantly associated with higher OHS knowledge scores. Discussion The findings demonstrate that OHS knowledge cannot be adequately characterized through a simple immigrant/non-immigrant distinction. Differences associated with settlement duration, residency status, and previous training highlight important heterogeneity among construction workers and may help identify OHS educational and prevention needs. Future research should evaluate whether targeted interventions addressing these differences improve safety practices and occupational health outcomes.

items.title: On Deploying Large Language Models for Streamlining Process Quality Quantification in HRC Remanufacturing
items.abstract: Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) plays a crucial role in managing the uncertainty of remanufacturing by enabling the needed flexibility and reconfigurability. However, a systematic evaluation approach of the remanufacturing system design is essential before deploying new HRC workstations. This paper presents a decision-making method, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs), to streamline the quantification of process quality metrics. By processing scenario descriptions, the LLM autonomously assigns metric values, enabling efficient, data-driven assessment of workstation configurations. The deployed system’s architecture, data pipeline, and prompt engineering strategy are also detailed. A case study from the household appliance sector is used to validate the approach leading to enhanced robustness, adaptability, and efficiency while also reducing manual engineering effort while supporting optimal workstation design.

items.title: One-Year Prediction of Vision-Threatening Diabetic Retinopathy Complications Using Multimodal Artificial Intelligence: A Multicenter Real-World Study
items.abstract: Abstract Current diabetic retinopathy management relies primarily on contemporaneous severity grading and does not directly quantify the short-term risk of vision-threatening complications. We developed and internally evaluated image-based artificial intelligence models for one-year prediction of diabetic retinopathy severity, proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) and center-involved diabetic macular edema (ci-DME) using retinal imaging acquired during routine care.The prospective multicenter EviRed cohort included 3,183 patients with diabetes, 8,520 visits and 16,509 eye-level observations collected across 14 French hospitals. Device-specific ensembles were developed for ultra-widefield color fundus photography (CLARUS500 and OPTOS) and OCT angiography (CIRRUS5000 and PLEX Elite9000). Predictions from individual images and both eyes were aggregated at the patient-visit level. Participants were partitioned at the patient level into adevelopment set (65\%) and a held-out test set (35\%).For prediction of diabetic retinopathy severity at the subsequent annual visit, OPTOS and CLARUS500 achieved quadratic weighted kappa values of 0.866 (95\% confidence interval, 0.842--0.878) and 0.852 (0.830--0.877), respectively. For incident ci-DME, CIRRUS5000 achieved the highest discrimination (AUC, 0.826; 0.770--0.878), whereas PLEX Elite9000 yielded the highest AUC point estimate for incident PDR (0.877; 0.807--0.950). Late fusion did not consistently outperform the strongest device-specific model. In secondary complete-case analyses, observed ci-DME incidence increased across quartiles of the image-derived risk score, reaching 19.7--30.4\% in the highest-risk quartile. AI models also achieved higher AUC point estimates than unassisted expert risk assessments for both complications, although these comparisons were exploratory.Retinal imaging acquired at a single routine-care visit therefore contains information associated with diabetic retinopathy severity and vision-threatening complications one year later. These findings support image-based short-term risk stratification, while external validation, calibration and prospective clinical utility assessment remain necessary before deployment.

items.title: Online Review Generation in the Digital Age: A Meta-Analytic Study of Online Review Behavior
items.abstract: A large body of literature on online review generation has investigated various antecedents to online review characteristics. However, the mixed and even contradictory findings in this domain have hampered a clear understanding of consumers’ online review behavior for both researchers and practitioners, thereby complicating actionable strategies. To address this issue, we conduct a comprehensive meta-analysis of 154 independent samples from 152 empirical papers, synthesizing the relationships between 28 antecedent factors and 12 review features, which we categorize into rating-based (evaluative) and non-rating (expressive) dimensions. Our results indicate that rating attributes are dominantly driven by stable reviewer tendencies and market-level reputation cues, whereas non-rating features—such as text length and image inclusion—are primarily influenced by reviewer social embeddedness and platform engagement. Crucially, we identify that inconsistencies in prior literature can be explained by critical boundary conditions, including platform type (business-hosted vs. third-party), goods type (service vs. tangible), and cultural background (Asia vs. North America). By distinguishing between evaluative and expressive review components, our study reconciles mixed findings and uncovers underlying mechanisms such as expectation-based evaluation and self-presentation. The findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for empirical model specification and offer actionable insights for retailers and platforms to optimize reputation management and system design. Ultimately, our work offers a holistic framework for understanding online review behavior and proposes a rich agenda for future research in the digital marketplace.

items.title: OpenConsult, an Open-Source Fully Local AI Scribe With Live Decision Support: Development and Formative Evaluation
items.abstract: Abstract Background. Ambient clinical AI — software that listens to a consultation and drafts the clinical note, often called an AI scribe — is now a flagship use of artificial intelligence in healthcare. Most tools delivering it are proprietary and cloud-based: consultation audio leaves the building, errors cannot be independently characterised, and the clinician who signs the note answers for output nobody outside the vendor can examine. Open, fully local alternatives that a clinician or researcher can inspect, run and modify remain rare. Objective. This paper reports OpenConsult, an open-source AI scribe with live clinical decision support that runs entirely on one machine in the consulting room and is inspectable end to end, and describes its formative evaluation. Methods. Evaluation was formative and used synthetic consultations only (scripted and acted). Automated tests ran fifteen scripted consultations with pre-written marking schemes, checking transcription quality gates, the urgency alarm’s behaviour across emergency and routine scripts, and whether every cited claim in a note points to a real transcript line. Five acted consultations followed in a real consulting room, and the AI assistants that built the system ran an adversarial security audit under the developer’s direction. The work is reported against the applicable DECIDE-AI items, one stage before live clinical evaluation. Results. OpenConsult is a fully local, open-source consultation assistant, built by a practising general practitioner directing AI coding assistants, running on a single consumer graphics card. It transcribes the consultation live and separates the speakers, drafts a structured clinical note with every sentence linked to its supporting transcript words, runs live decision support whose urgency alarm is shown only to the doctor, drafts referral letters, and offers a supervised spoken history-taking mode. In generated notes, 301 of 302 citations pointed to real transcript lines — an existence check, with clinical faithfulness unmeasured pending independent rating; the one uncited claim was flagged for manual checking. The urgency alarm fired in all eight scripted emergencies and stayed silent in six of seven routine consultations. Five acted consultations surfaced five defects the automated checks had missed, four of them serious; all were fixed, each pinned by a regression test. The security audit returned twelve findings, including one critical vulnerability, fixed and verified before any public exposure. Conclusions. OpenConsult is a working, auditable proof of concept — not yet a validated clinical tool — released for research and education only, with real patient care out of scope. It is intended as an open research instrument: it records whether the reviewing clinician opened the cited evidence before approving, how long review takes, and every revision of its decision support, making human review of ambient clinical AI measurable. Independent, prospective evaluation is required before any step toward care.

items.title: Opportunities and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence Use in Secondary School Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering the everyday work of secondary schools. Teachers encounter AI-based tools both in classroom organisation and in feedback or adaptation tasks. As these tools become more visible in school practice, their educational role and practical value need to be examined in relation to the conditions of real classrooms. This is especially relevant in classes with varied learning characteristics, where students differ in pace and readiness to participate. In these settings, AI may help teachers adapt instructional material and provide more individualised support. Its value, however, depends on professional judgement and on how each tool is connected to pedagogical purpose. This paper examines opportunities and challenges related to the use of artificial intelligence in secondary education. The planned study will use teachers’ accounts to examine how AI tools are understood and used in secondary school practice. It is designed as a qualitative inquiry based on semi-structured interviews with secondary education teachers, with the interview material examined thematically. Through teachers’ accounts, the study will explore how AI is understood in relation to lesson preparation and student support, while also examining what makes its use difficult in day-to-day teaching. The paper approaches AI as a tool whose usefulness depends on classroom context and teachers’ pedagogical decisions.

items.title: Participation without power: urban biodiversity plans exclude the communities most affected by biodiversity loss
items.abstract: Urban biodiversity loss is increasingly framed as a governance challenge with intertwined ecological and social dimensions, yet little is known about who participates in local biodiversity planning, what authority that participation carries, and whether plans recognize and address disproportionate harms. This study presents the first comparative analysis at this scale of participation in Local Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (LBSAPs), examining 98 plans from 98 municipalities across 26 countries. Using a hybrid methodology combining large language model-assisted verbatim extraction with manual coding (96.4% extraction accuracy), plans were assessed across four dimensions: participant recognition, participatory mechanisms, authorship, and transparency. Of the 98 plans, 71 (72%) documented some participatory mechanism, but only 18 (18%) granted participants any authority over plan content, and only 2 (2%) shared control over resources. Authorship was concentrated in city governments (93 of 98 plans), and 39 cities (40%) provided no transparency about participatory processes. Knowledge-holder positioning was dominated by scientists (M = 0.60 on a 0–1 scale) while Indigenous peoples (M = 0.08), marginalized groups (M = 0.01), and youth (M = 0.03) were systematically excluded. A distributive analysis revealed a marginalized-specific redress gap: 16 plans recognized marginalized groups as bearing environmental harm, but only 4 of those plans offered programmatic response; a 75% recognition-without-remedy rate not seen for any other actor type. These findings indicate that prevailing LBSAP governance architectures may constrain conservation effectiveness, by excluding the situated knowledge of communities most affected by biodiversity loss, and may reproduce environmental injustice, by acknowledging disproportionate harms without acting on them. Governance reforms that meaningfully redistribute participatory authority are needed to advance both biodiversity outcomes and equitable urban conservation.

items.title: Patent Application: HYBRID CLASSICAL-QUANTUM PROCESS FOR THE IN SILICO RECOMBINATION OF PLANT GENOMES WITH EVALUATION BY MEANS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
items.abstract: Plant genomics with a hybrid classical-quantum model Artificial intelligence and quantum computing for the digital design of plant genomes Italian patent application no. 102026000034324, filed on 18 November 2026. Inventor, applicant and sole rights holder: Paolo Ciccolella. This invention proposes combining artificial intelligence and quantum computing to explore possible combinations of plant DNA and identify those worth investigating further. For businesses interested in plant genomics, the idea is to provide early guidance for computational design: turning a vast number of possibilities into selected, evaluated and documented digital candidates. The challenge is easy to picture. If DNA is a large instruction book, studying alternative versions of some passages means comparing many combinations. Three alternatives for each of twenty regions already produce more than three billion possibilities. The method tackles this complexity by dividing the work between a classical computer, two AI models and a quantum search component. HOW THE HYBRID MODEL WORKS The idea is to choose one alternative for each DNA region being studied, put the choices together and evaluate the resulting combination. Everything happens on a computer. The process follows six steps. • Prepare the data. The computer starts with a digital version of the plant’s DNA, called a reference genome. It identifies the regions to study and organises the available alternative sequences for each one, recording where they come from. • Give each alternative an initial score. The first AI model examines each alternative separately. Having learned from other cases, it can provide guidance before any complete combination in the new case has been evaluated. The computer also measures similarity between the ends of sequences that will be placed next to one another. These scores and measurements define the selection problem. [B12] • Search for combinations. The quantum component receives this problem expressed in numbers. It uses QAOA, an algorithm whose role is to propose combinations while seeking to favour those with better scores. Qubits represent the possible choices; the DNA sequences remain on the classical computer, which sets and updates the algorithm’s parameters. [B11] • Evaluate the whole combination. The computer checks that each combination selects exactly one alternative per region and assembles valid choices into a digital candidate. The second AI model evaluates the complete candidate, including relationships between its parts that the first AI model could not observe when examining them separately. • Guide the next search. The system compares the overall evaluation with the score predicted at the start and uses the difference to update the search. When only a few results are available, it limits the correction’s influence to avoid relying too heavily on sparse information. • Return verifiable proposals. For each selected candidate, the system retains the chosen sequences, their provenance and the evaluations performed. It also records a digital fingerprint, a code used to check the content. Researchers can reconstruct the proposal and understand how it was selected. If necessary data are missing, the system flags this. A concrete example: the patent uses the digital reference for Micro-Tom tomato and considers three regions, each with three alternatives created for the test. There are 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 possible combinations. The search uses a nine-qubit quantum circuit simulated on a classical computer. This tests the computational method without producing plants. [B14] INDUSTRIAL APPLICATIONS The patent describes the production of verifiable digital representations of candidate genomes. Its industrial role lies in designing and selecting hypotheses, ahead of experimental work. Applications across sectors require data and models suited to the objectives under study. • NGT and assisted evolution techniques. NGTs, or new genomic techniques, include approaches known in Italy as TEA, meaning assisted evolution techniques, which enable targeted changes to genetic material. The proposed method could support research by comparing genomic hypotheses before experimental work. For seed and biotechnology companies, the prospect is to build a reasoned set of digital candidates for further investigation within NGT/TEA programmes. • Seed industry and variety development. For seed companies and research teams, the method could support the preliminary selection of combinations for further study. Research objectives could include drought or salinity tolerance, disease resistance and yield stability. Its contribution would be to establish research priorities while preserving the reasoning behind them. • Fresh produce and food processing. Computational design could focus on commercial characteristics such as product quality, shelf life and processing suitability. Tomato, pepper and aubergine are examples of supply chains that future projects could address, connecting growers’ and processors’ needs with the criteria used to evaluate candidates. • Nutraceuticals and plant ingredients. One possible development concerns plants of interest for functional ingredients, extracts and bioactive compounds. The method could explore genomic combinations in programmes focused, for example, on pigments or plant metabolites, providing documented candidates to guide subsequent analysis. • Plant biotechnology and industrial raw materials. For crops intended for oils, fibres or biomass, the method could help compare genomic hypotheses against supply chain objectives. Reconstructible digital records would support information exchange between teams developing the models and those planning subsequent experimental work. • Bioinformatics and computing centres. The most direct application is within the information systems of laboratories, computing centres and plant genomics businesses. The process could underpin software modules or analytical services that explore combinations and return candidates with scores and execution logs, integrating quantum search into the workflow. items.title: Patient perceptions of artificial intelligence in MRI reconstruction: A mixed methods study from a single NHS trust
items.abstract: Introduction As part of a strategy to increase magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) capacity, the UK government funded the purchase of manufacturer artificial intelligence (AI) MRI image reconstruction software on MRI scanners. It aimed to reduce scan duration without compromising image quality and has been widely installed on clinical MRI scanners across the UK. Methods This is a mixed methods study, using an initial questionnaire to quantify opinions followed by focus groups of responders to further explore their views on technical issues. Patient views on the use of AI in MRI image reconstruction for reducing acquisition times, and more generally in their MRI pathway, were assessed. Results Study participants prefer improved image quality over faster acquisition times. If reducing acquisition times with AI, they feel it should only be used if extremely accurate images can be ascertained. They are uncomfortable with the use of manufacturer AI software for image reconstruction where accuracy is not stated and would like to be told about the use of AI in MRI. Conclusions Many participants felt that manufacturer AI software for MRI image reconstruction may be used only if a high accuracy is demonstrated, and if the training data is representative of the patient population, to not exacerbate health inequalities. This information is not currently given by manufacturers, which made the patient representatives concerned. Implication for practice •Local validation of AI image reconstruction software may make patients more confident about its use. •AI patient information materials should be accessible and discuss accuracy, and radiographers can be trained to help inform and reassure patients. •Engagement with all clinical stakeholders in MRI should be undertaken to understand their views on AI, and how manufacturer AI software should be implemented.

items.abstract: Over the past decade, the innovative convergence of cloud computing, natural language processing (NLP), and large language models (LLM) has triggered a paradigm shift in human-computer interaction. This study aims to conceptually review and propose a research design to objectively analyze the effect of security and privacy perceptions on the use of AI as a venting medium. The proposed method is a conceptual quantitative research design with a correlational approach, planned for Generation Z respondents. Based on a literature synthesis of referenced studies, the findings indicate a highly significant positive correlation between dispositional shame and self-disclosure to artificial intelligence (r = 0.337, p < 0.001, n = 182). The conceptual review concludes that AI operates effectively as a complementary screening instrument but risks triggering an atrophy of social resilience, thus necessitating juridical protection through the Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP).

items.title: People Before Algorithms: Integrating Ignatian Wisdom to Foster Human-Centric Corporate Practices in the AI Era
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has changed businesses aiming at increasing the efficiency of operations. This technological revolution, considered meritorious, is not exempt from limitations. The prime focus is shifted from people to technology. In the fourth industrial revolution, the processes are automated in manufacturing through advanced technologies. Industry 5.0 emerged as a new paradigm where humans are prioritized along with the adoption of technology. Human centeredness is always at the heart of spirituality. Among the various forms of spirituality, Ignatian spirituality is structured and more popular. The challenges posed by Artificial Intelligence and digital transformation can be addressed by imbibing Ignatian spirituality. There are limited studies connecting Ignatian spirituality and Industry 5.0. This prompted the researchers to do this conceptual study. An extensive literature review on the areas of artificial intelligence, Industry 5.0 and Ignatian spirituality was done. An Ignatian framework is proposed to implement human friendly AI practices. This paper will guide business leaders, technology designers, and organizational development experts to design systems that promote human-centric approaches in the AI-driven world.

items.title: Perceived Benefits and Reported Uses of Generative AI for Accessibility: An Exploratory Survey of Minnesota Educators
items.abstract: Digital inclusion with generative AI depends not only on educators’ access to tools but on how they use them. Comparing the benefits educators perceive with the uses they report may reveal gaps between what educators believe AI can do and how they use it in teaching. In this exploratory secondary analysis of survey data from 293 Minnesota PK-12 and higher education educators, we compared endorsement of improved accessibility for diverse learners as a benefit of generative AI with reported use of AI to enhance accessibility for students with disabilities. Because the items differ in scope and target population, the comparison describes response proportions, not a failure to act on a belief. Among 160 AI-using educators who answered both items, 133 (83.1%) endorsed the benefit and 51 (31.9%) reported the use (McNemar exact p < 0.001). Subgroup differences were not detected, though power was limited. Among all AI users, self-rated competence was associated with reported accessibility use (44.0% vs. 27.9%; adjusted OR = 2.31, 95% CI [1.13, 4.73]); among endorsers, the estimate was imprecise. Keyword-selected open-ended responses more often described general differentiation and language support than disability-specific use. We discuss measurement implications and propose supports as hypotheses for evaluation.

items.title: Perceived impact of generative artificial intelligence on clinical learning and decision-making among internal medicine residents in Ethiopia: a mixed- methods study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical training, but evidence from African residency programs is scarce. We assessed how internal medicine residents in Ethiopia use GenAI and how they perceive its impact on clinical learning and clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study consisting of a national cross-sectional online survey of internal medicine residents (June to August 2026), followed by two focus group discussions (FGDs) with 10 residents at two universities (September 2026) to explain the survey findings. Perceived impact was measured with five-point Likert items and two composite scores (learning, five items; decision-making, eight items). Associations with frequency of use were tested with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. FGD data were organized deductively into categories based on the survey topics. Results Of 252 respondents from 18 institutions, 98.8% had used GenAI and 75.4% used it daily; ChatGPT was used by 91.6% of users. The mean composite score for perceived impact on clinical learning was 3.83 out of 5 (70.7% high) and for clinical decision-making 3.86 out of 5 (67.7% high). Agreement was highest for improved differential diagnosis (90.8%), learning efficiency (81.9%) and support for self-directed learning (79.5%), and lowest for ward-round performance (64.3%) and confidence in complex cases (71.4%). Daily use was more frequent among residents with more than three hours of daily internet use (82.3% versus 66.7% to 67.4%; p = 0.024) and was not associated with age, sex, marital status, year of residency, device access or formal training. In the FGDs, residents described GenAI as a fast, supportive tool for learning and clinical work, as an aid to reasoning and not a replacement for physician judgment, and as a possible threat to independent learning. Conclusions Residents perceive GenAI as helpful for self-directed learning and diagnostic reasoning while keeping final responsibility for clinical decisions. These findings reflect perceptions and not measured outcomes, so objective evaluation of its effects on learning and clinical performance is needed.

items.title: Performance of Multimodal Large Language Models and Humans on Curated AI-Generated Intraoral Images
items.abstract: Introduction and aims To evaluate the authenticity detection performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) using real and AI-generated intraoral photographs and to compare their performance with human evaluators with different levels of dental experience. Methods A dataset of 1,000 intraoral photographs (500 real and 500 AI-generated) across 5 standardised views was constructed from single-institution clinical images and the publicly available AI-Hub dataset. GPT-5.1 (OpenAI), Claude Opus 4.5 (Anthropic), and Gemini 3.0 Pro (Google) evaluated all images through vendor APIs. Human evaluation was conducted using a stratified random subset of 200 images by fourth-year dental students, dentists with ≤5 years, and dentists with ≥6 years of clinical experience (n = 5 per group). Results In the 200-image subset, dentists with ≥6 years showed the highest performance (accuracy: 0.740; F1-score: 0.675), followed by dentists with ≤5 years (accuracy: 0.690; F1-score: 0.557). Across the 1,000-image dataset, GPT-5.1 achieved the highest performance among the MLLMs (accuracy: 0.646; F1-score: 0.452), whereas Claude Opus 4.5 showed the lowest (accuracy: 0.571; F1-score: 0.249). All groups demonstrated substantially higher accuracy for real images than for the curated, visually plausible AI-generated images, with the MLLMs combining near-perfect specificity (0.998-1.000) and low recall (0.142-0.292), whereas human specificity was 0.890-0.990 and recall 0.390-0.540. The mandibular occlusal view showed the lowest accuracy among the MLLM groups. Conclusion Current MLLMs showed lower performance than experienced human evaluator panels, with limited recall for the AI-generated images in this study, suggesting that they are not yet suitable as standalone authenticity detection tools in dentistry. Clinical Relevance The increasing visual realism of generative artificial intelligence-generated intraoral photographs suggests that authenticity cannot be judged from visual inspection alone, and robust validation is needed before such images are used as clinical records, teaching material, or training data for artificial intelligence.

items.title: Performing Trust in AI-Generated Journalism: Transparency, Authorship and Accountability in Algorithmic News Content
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in news production, journalistic credibility can no longer be understood only through audience trust in machine-generated content. This article examines how AI-generated and AI-assisted journalism is made to appear trustworthy through textual, editorial, and institutional cues. Drawing on qualitative comparative content analysis of a 37-text corpus comprising 14 AI-generated or AI-assisted news articles, 14 human-written comparison articles, four newsroom AI policy documents, and five correction or controversy-related texts, the study analyses how credibility is constructed through authorship, disclosure, sourcing, human oversight, correction practice, and institutional framing. The findings show that AI-assisted journalism can reproduce familiar signs of professional news, including factual tone, structured formats, institutional attribution, and data specificity. Yet these cues do not necessarily make editorial responsibility visible. The article develops the concept of algorithmic credibility performance to explain how AI journalism assembles trustworthiness through uneven arrangements of transparency, evidence, and accountability before audiences respond.

items.title: Peripheral Inflammatory Indices in Major Depressive Disorder: Clinical Associations and Explainable Machine Learning
items.abstract: Background: The clinical relevance of routinely available peripheral inflammatory indices in major depressive disorder (MDD) remains uncertain, particularly regarding recent suicide attempts, depressive symptom severity, and their discriminative performance. This study investigated these associations using conventional statistical analyses and explainable machine learning. Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included 86 patients with MDD and 80 healthy controls. Six blood-derived inflammatory indices were examined for between-group differences and associations with recent suicide attempts and depressive symptom severity. Individual-marker discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis, while three ensemble machine-learning models were evaluated using nested cross-validation and compared with MHR alone. Explainable artificial intelligence methods were applied to interpret model predictions. Results: Patients with MDD showed higher MHR, NHR, SIRI, and AISI values than controls. Recent suicide attempts were associated with higher SII, SIRI, and AISI, and these associations persisted after adjustment for age and sex; lower LHR was observed only in the unadjusted comparison and was not significant after adjustment. No inflammatory index was significantly associated with depressive symptom severity. MHR demonstrated the strongest individual discrimination. Machine-learning models showed modest discriminative performance without clear improvement over MHR alone, and feature-importance analyses consistently highlighted MHR. Conclusions: Here we show that peripheral inflammatory indices exhibit distinct observational associations with MDD and recent suicidal behavior. However, their diagnostic and predictive clinical utility remains unestablished and requires prospective, adequately controlled, independently validated studies.

items.title: Persistent Records Without Decoding Support: When a Record Survives and Its Reading Does Not
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Persistent Records Without Decoding Support, a mechanism by which a record outlasts the conventions, skills, or equipment needed to read it. The paper distinguishes two requirements for practical access. Recoverability concerns whether a reader can extract the marks or data. Intelligibility concerns whether the reader can establish what they mean. Each depends on the support available to a particular reader at a particular time. The documented case is the decipherment of Linear B. Clay tablets from Knossos and Pylos preserved palace accounts for more than 3,000 years. Before decipherment, scholars could copy the signs and recognize some pictured objects while the words beside them remained unreadable. Building on work by Alice Kober and Emmett Bennett, Michael Ventris identified the language as an early form of Greek in 1952. A tablet discovered later at Pylos helped confirm the reading. The words for two tripods appeared beside a tripod sign and the numeral 2. The 1986 BBC Domesday Project provides a contrast. By 2002, few working systems could read its videodiscs. A surviving drive supplied data for the CAMiLEON emulation demonstration, and preservation teams carried material onto newer systems. Access had become precarious while the means of reading still existed. The paper places this case alongside Jeff Rothenberg’s account of digital obsolescence and his proposal to emulate older computers. Part of the Records and Circulation series within On Human Modeling, the paper also offers a distinction relevant to human–AI interaction. An archive might preserve an AI system’s responses as sequences of token IDs. A later reader could copy every number, yet recovering the wording would depend on finding or reconstructing the mapping from those numbers to text.

items.title: Perspectives: A Tale of Three Plots: Advancing narrative theorising in organisation and management research
items.abstract: Narrative theorising (rather than theorising based on constructs and models) is much called for in qualitative research in management and organisation studies. Despite this, how to emplot, i.e. the process of configuring fragmented events into coherent and meaningful accounts with the objective of sensemaking and understanding remains underexplored. This Perspectives piece showcases recent exemplars illustrating how we can practice narrative theorising using three distinct styles: historical, metaphorical, and discursive narratives. Since narrative theorising is commonly observed in single-case studies, we begin our exploration by drawing on six such articles published in Organization Studies to demonstrate how these styles foreground the temporal evolution of phenomena, bridge between multiple divergent accounts, or highlight conflicts between competing discourses to construct theoretical accounts and understanding. We illustrate each style in terms of its distinctive form, set of paradigmatic assumptions, analytical moves, and intended aims, with the overall aim of advancing the potential of narrative theorising in organisation and management research.

items.title: Phantom Networks: Window on Agency in Social Mechanisms
items.abstract: Our goal is to offer proof of concept for the idea that behavioral networks emerging with and beyond assigned treatment networks in experiments can provide a valuable window on agency. We call these often unobserved behavioral structures phantom networks. Most evidence of agency is entangled with audience—what people recall, how others attribute, or who is seen to act. We strip that away to observe agency directly in the ties participants build within and beyond what they are assigned. Their deviation from assignment is not error but structure in action, a behavioral trace of agency. We offer three exhibits of that “behavioral deviation” revealing agency in gendered brokerage, rival brokerage, and structural reproduction. Across the three exhibits, behavioral deviation shows how a team works (sometimes in surprising ways), not how well the team works. Teams perform as expected in theory, but the behavior responsible for their performance is made more apparent by watching behavioral deviation. We close with a summary proof of concept and discussion of next steps for particularly promising future work. items.title: Predicting Dynamic Modulus of Asphalt Mixtures Using Explainable Artificial Intelligence Techniques: A Design Optimization Application
items.abstract: Abstract Dynamic Modulus (DM) is a critical characteristic for the design of Hot Mix Asphalt (HMA), which is currently determined through complex empirical models. This study applies advanced explainable Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques to predict DM, enhance the understanding of the factors affecting it, and support design optimization applications. An extensive experimental dataset was used that included a variety of aggregate gradations, different types of bituminous binders, volumetric characteristics, and test conditions in terms of test temperature and loading rate. Eight different predictive models were developed, ranging from simple linear regression to advanced machine learning models, including Support Vector Machines (SVM) and ensemble techniques, using a random selection scheme for cross-validation. Comparison of model performance indicated that the best performing model was the Cubic SVM, with an R 2 = 0.96 and RMSE = 2.22 × 10 5 psi, representing an approximate 39% reduction in error compared to the baseline linear regression. Explainable AI analysis revealed that phase angle was the most significant parameter in predicting DM, followed by aggregate gradation and binder characteristics. Overall, the findings show that the DM of HMA is influenced by complex nonlinear interactions among multiple factors. The AI-based models provided higher predictive accuracy and insights into interactions among material properties, supporting the development of optimized asphalt mix design guidelines for durable pavements.

items.title: Predictive performance of artificial intelligence and machine learning for mosquito vector surveillance worldwide: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background Mosquito-borne diseases remain a major global public health challenge, with expanding geographic distribution driven by climate change, urbanization, and environmental modifications. Accurate forecasting of mosquito vector populations is essential for effective surveillance and control. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) approaches have emerged as promising tools for modelling complex, nonlinear relationships in vector ecology. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the predictive performance of AI and ML models applied to mosquito vector surveillance worldwide and to summarize comparative evidence with traditional statistical methods where directly reported. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus was conducted up to August 2025. Studies modelling mosquito vectors (Aedes, Culex, Anopheles) using AI/ML techniques were included. Data on study characteristics, modelling approaches, predictors, and performance metrics (e.g., AUC, sensitivity, specificity, RMSE, R 2 ) were extracted. Results were primarily synthesized descriptively because of substantial methodological and clinical/ecological heterogeneity. Exploratory random-effects meta-analyses were conducted for commonly reported performance metrics, with pooled estimates interpreted alongside measures of between-study heterogeneity and prediction intervals. Risk of bias was assessed using a PROBAST-informed assessment adapted to the ecological and entomological context. Results Seventy-one studies were included, spanning diverse geographic regions and ecological settings. Random Forest was the most frequently used algorithm. Reported predictive performance varied substantially across studies and prediction tasks, with AUC values ranging from 0.61 to 0.99. Exploratory quantitative syntheses showed exceptionally high between-study heterogeneity, limiting the generalizability of pooled performance estimates. Most studies relied on internal validation, with limited use of external validation, further limiting assessment of model performance across independent surveillance settings. Conclusions AI and ML approaches show potential for supporting mosquito vector surveillance, but reported predictive performance varies substantially across prediction tasks, taxa, ecological settings, and validation frameworks. The extreme heterogeneity observed across studies limits the generalizability of pooled performance estimates and precludes broad conclusions regarding the predictive performance of AI/ML approaches across surveillance settings. Methodological standardization, transparent reporting, external validation across independent settings, and direct comparisons with conventional statistical approaches are needed to establish the reliability and real-world applicability of these models. items.title: Preservation of Reopening Conditions Through Provisional Closure: How an Inquiry Can Stop With a Route Back
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Preservation of Reopening Conditions Through Provisional Closure, an account of how inquiry can end for the purposes of action while retaining a planned route for later reopening. The mechanism consists in preserving an unresolved dependency, a condition that would warrant reconsideration, and an accessible route through which relevant evidence can be detected, connected to the closed question, and brought to someone able to act. The paper assesses provisional closure by whether the specified trigger can be detected, linked to the prior issue, and translated into a feasible step of reopening. It distinguishes retaining these conditions from their subsequent use: storage alone does not ensure monitoring, recognition, authority, or action. It also separates preserving a route back from the later conversion of detected discrepancy into effective revision. The account concerns consequential unresolved dependencies and does not require every conclusion to remain provisional. The mechanism is situated alongside Charles S. Peirce’s account of inquiry as the settlement of doubt and examined through two documented cases. Olympic anti-doping sample storage preserves material for later reanalysis when new information or improved detection methods become available. Japan’s conditional, time-limited approval of HeartSheet required follow-up and reapplication with survival evidence; the submitted analysis did not demonstrate superiority on its primary endpoint, and regular approval was refused. These cases are interpreted through published studies and institutional reports, with attention to the retained evidence, review conditions, and authority required to reopen a settled decision. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines who retains and monitors reopening conditions, who can authorize reconsideration, and who bears the continuing cost of maintaining a route back. Potential applications in human–AI research include preserving assumption records, specifying review triggers, routing later evidence to responsible decision makers, and designing processes through which decisions can return to active inquiry.

items.title: Process Before Prompting: A Pedagogical Framework for Preserving Evaluative Responsibility When Integrating Generative AI into Creative Media Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can expand the range of candidate solutions available during design exploration, but it can also obscure whether students have engaged in the iterative design reasoning and evaluative judgement that studio teaching is intended to develop. This article examines how GenAI can be integrated into creative media education without displacing the cognitive processes through which creative expertise is cultivated. It draws on design research, automation literature, and cognitive load theory, alongside illustrative teaching cases spanning undergraduate and postgraduate animation, visual effects, and game design curricula at Auckland University of Technology and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University. We argue that the educational value of GenAI depends not on the sophistication of its outputs alone, but on whether students retain responsibility for evaluative judgement throughout the design process. We propose Process Before Prompting, a pedagogical framework intended to preserve this responsibility within human-led cycles of divergence, convergence, and appreciative judgement. Students establish an initial creative intention before engaging with GenAI and remain responsible for interpreting, refining, and selecting among both human- and AI-generated candidates. This framework offers practical guidance for scaffolding independent judgement and assessing evidence of iterative design reasoning within existing studio teaching practices.

items.title: Production-source disclosures, higher-order creative attributions, and audience reception of two-dimensional animation: evidence from a randomized source-disclosure experiment
items.abstract: Introduction Attribution theory explains how audiences use observable information to infer otherwise unobservable agents and processes behind creative work. This study applied this perspective to examine how production-source disclosures influence source-role perceptions, higher-order creative attributions, and audience reception of two-dimensional animation. Methods In a randomized experiment, 626 adults were assigned to one of four production-source disclosure conditions—undisclosed, human-made, human–AI collaborative, or AI-led—while viewing the same three animation clips, all of which were actually produced through human–AI collaboration. We examined between-condition differences in source-role perceptions, higher-order creative attributions, and audience-reception outcomes, as well as concurrent associations between higher-order creative attributions and audience reception. Results The disclosures clearly differentiated participants’ perceptions of AI and human involvement. Perceived creative effort was statistically significant before correction but did not meet the α = 0.05 criterion after Holm adjustment ( p = 0.0502); the only corrected contrast indicated lower perceived creative effort in the human–AI collaborative condition than in the human-made condition. No statistically reliable omnibus between-condition differences emerged for perceived authorship, perceived emotional authenticity, artistic evaluation, situational immersion, or viewing and recommendation intention. Higher-order creative attributions were positively associated with all three audience-reception indicators in concurrent analyses, although the strong correlation between perceived emotional authenticity and situational immersion warrants caution about measurement overlap. Discussion The findings indicate that the diagnosticity of a production-source cue depends on the judgment target: the disclosures clearly reorganized perceived production roles but did not yield statistically reliable corresponding differences across most higher-order creative attributions or reception outcomes. The attribution–reception relations represent concurrent covariation rather than causal mediation. Because the three clips were presented in a fixed order, material and order effects cannot be separated, and the equivalence analyses did not establish negligible between-condition differences.

items.title: Proposal of Facial Shiatsu Massage Exergame System with AI-Based Quiz Generator for Smart Healthcare
items.abstract: The World Health Organization (WHO) identifies high blood pressure (hypertension) as a major global public health concern and a significant risk factor for cardiovascular diseases. Therefore, facial Shiatsu massage can be a good solution to alleviate them. However, most people are not only unfamiliar with the locations of acupressure points for proper massage but also lack motivation to conduct it regularly. In this paper, we propose a facial Shiatsu massage exergame system as an effective approach to solve these conditions together. The system runs on a low-cost PC with a camera, provides a simple quiz on a selective topic, and recognizes an answer gesture of a player to select one choice to each question. A generative AI-based quiz generator is implemented to automatically generate quiz questions across different categories providing flexible and varied educational content for the proposed smart healthcare exergame system. An answer gesture is defined for pressing a proper acupressure point with an index finger, which is recognized by applying a MediaPipe library to a user’s face image taken by a PC camera. In this paper, four gestures are implemented to select one of the four choices in each question. For accuracy evaluation, first, we implemented the answer gesture recognition program and investigated the gesture recognition accuracy. Then, for effectiveness evaluation, we implemented the quiz generator using Ollama, produced quizzes on Japanese History, Simple Arithmetic, Indonesian Words, and Taiwan Geography with 50 questions for each topic, and asked 20 persons to use the system. For each user, we measured health condition-related indices such as blood pressure, body temperature, and facial skin moisture level before and after the system use by each person. In addition, we conducted a questionnaire and calculated the Usability and User Experience score. These results indicate the potential feasibility of the proposed system.

items.title: Psychometric Comparison of the NASA-TLX and PROS-TLX for Myoelectric Prosthesis Use
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Prosthesis users report high cognitive workload, or the mental effort needed to achieve task performance. The NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) is the most common subjective workload measure. However, it was developed for general human–machine interfaces and may not capture prosthesis-specific demands. The recently proposed Prosthesis Task Load Index (PROS-TLX) includes additional domains relevant to prosthesis use, yet its psychometric properties have not been established. This study compared the convergent validity, test-retest reliability, and measurement error of the NASA-TLX and PROS-TLX across two groups.Methods: Ten individuals without limb difference performed a timed reach-and-grasp task using a myoelectric prosthetic emulator in both a physical and virtual environment. Additionally, ten individuals with upper limb difference performed an accuracy- and time-based activity of daily living using their customary myoelectric, multi-grip prosthesis. Both groups completed two sessions at least a week apart and rated workload using the NASA-TLX and the PROS-TLX in both sessions. Because the PROS-TLX has more total subscales, we modified the scoring of the PROS-TLX to align it with the NASA-TLX. For both surveys, total workload scores were a weighted average of the subscales, ranging from low (0) to high (100). We compared total workload scores between the surveys using Pearson's correlation and calculated the intraclass correlation coefficients, measurement error, and minimum detectable change for each survey. We also explored the role of session number, survey, and task environment on the survey subscales and the relationships between subscales and task performance outcomes.Results: For emulator users, the PROS-TLX and NASA-TLX total workload scores were moderately correlated in session 1 (r>0.63), suggesting good convergent validity. However, for prosthesis users, the surveys were weakly correlated in session 1 (r=0.13). The PROS-TLX demonstrated higher test–retest reliability point estimates (ICC=0.44–0.83) and lower measurement error (SEM=7.43-10.79) than NASA-TLX (ICC=0.18-0.45, SEM=10.52-17.29), though the confidence intervals were large. The prosthesis-specific subscale of uncertainty varied by task environment and correlated with performance outcomes.Conclusions: The PROS-TLX adds prosthesis-specific contributors to workload to the NASA-TLX with higher reliability and lower measurement error estimates, but wide confidence intervals limit conclusions. Larger studies in prosthesis users are needed.

items.title: QPAFusion: Query-Guided Radar Refinement and Prior-Guided Adaptive Fusion for Marine Object Detection
items.abstract: Accurate marine target detection is essential for maritime situational awareness and safe navigation by unmanned surface vehicles. However, uneven radar returns and uncertain spatial correspondence complicate radar–camera fusion, while input-level integration does not explicitly adapt subsequent feature processing to local radar evidence. We propose QPAFusion, which refines multi-scale features through query-guided local radar sampling and adaptively aggregates feature branches using radar priors. On the WaterScenes dataset, QPAFusion achieves 64.5%mAP50−−95 and 90.9%mAP50, exceeding the reported three-frame REVP fusion baseline by 2.0 and 2.1 percentage points, respectively, with mAP50 gains of 6.4 and 3.1 percentage points on the adverse-lighting and adverse-weather subsets. These results support combining local-radar refinement with adaptive feature aggregation for object detection on the water surface, with larger accuracy gains on the evaluated adverse-condition subsets.

items.title: Quality Assurance Framework for AI Governance and Integration in Higher Education Accreditation: A First Operational Model for Safe AI Integration
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming embedded in higher education systems, influencing teaching, assessment, research, and institutional decision-making. Despite the growing adoption of AI, existing governance approaches remain largely principle-based, emphasizing ethical guidelines such as transparency, accountability, and fairness without providing operational mechanisms for implementation within quality assurance (QA) and accreditation systems. This creates a critical gap between AI governance principles and the procedural structures through which educational quality and institutional accountability are evaluated. This study addresses this gap by developing an operational quality assurance framework to systematically integrate AI governance into a ten-step higher education accreditation lifecycle, with explicitly differentiated AI permission levels and defined boundaries for human evaluative authority. Using a conceptual and policy-synthesis approach, the study integrates global AI governance principles, established QA standards, and accreditation practices into a risk-based, human-centered governance model. The framework operationalizes AI governance and integration through a model that defines the role, boundaries, and permissible levels of AI use across each stage of the accreditation process. A central feature of the model is the explicit preservation of human decision-making authority in evaluative and high-stakes accreditation stages. The study reconceptualizes AI integration in higher education as a quality assurance and governance challenge rather than solely a technological innovation problem. By embedding AI governance and integrating it directly within accreditation processes, the proposed model provides a practical bridge between ethical principles and operational implementation. The proposed framework provides a structured basis for quality assurance agencies, regulators, and higher education institutions to consider risk-based AI governance within accreditation processes, with its feasibility, effectiveness, and transferability requiring further evaluation through implementation and empirical validation.

items.title: Quality-controlled synthetic oversampling for imbalanced tabular classification using large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Many tabular classification tasks involve imbalanced classes, but synthetic oversampling can produce rows that violate feature constraints or duplicate existing observations. We present QualSynth, a training-free framework that prompts a large language model to make sparse edits to real minority-class rows under data-derived feature constraints and a machine-readable output contract. A deterministic validation layer checks each candidate’s structure, values, and duplication before admitting it to the training set. We evaluated QualSynth on eight benchmark datasets with ten seeds against four synthetic oversamplers, including the widely used SMOTE, and class-weighted learning without augmentation. QualSynth achieved the highest F1 score among the synthetic oversamplers on four datasets, while SMOTE had the best average ranks. In equivalence tests, QualSynth and SMOTE differed by less than prespecified margins of 0.03 in F1 score and 0.02 in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). After correction for multiple comparisons, the only pairwise difference was higher ROC-AUC for QualSynth than for the diffusion model TabDDPM. Class weighting alone had the best overall ranks, and no augmentation strategy improved aggregate ROC-AUC over the unweighted reference. QualSynth is therefore a controlled, inspectable option for minority-class augmentation, with predictive utility comparable to SMOTE’s.

items.title: RamanGPT maps bidirectionally between crystal structures and Raman spectra of inorganic materials
items.abstract: Abstract Raman spectroscopy is one of the most accessible vibrational probes in materials laboratories, but its forward problem (structure to spectrum) is bottlenecked by the cost of density functional perturbation theory, and its inverse problem (spectrum to structure) typically relies on retrieval against curated references. We introduce RamanGPT, a deep-learning framework that addresses both directions for crystalline inorganic materials. The forward model, an Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network (ALIGNN), is trained on the 5,099-material Computational Raman Database and predicts 200-bin spectra over 50–1000 $$\hbox {cm}^{-1}$$ with 53.8% of the 509 held-out materials reaching an active-region cosine similarity of at least 0.354, capturing qualitative features of the target spectrum. The model also shows qualitative agreement with an experimental measurement of metallic 1T $$\hbox {VSe}_{2}$$ , a system absent from the training set. The inverse model fine-tunes DiffractGPT, a large language model already trained for diffraction-to-structure generation, via Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation on Raman-plus-formula prompts, recovering lattice parameters with mean absolute errors of 1.13–2.14 Å and reduced-formula consistency of 92.1% on 508 held-out materials, compared to 17.1% for a formula-conditioned retrieval baseline given identical inputs. A cosine-similarity matcher and an inverse $$\rightarrow$$ relax $$\rightarrow$$ forward consistency loop are deployed at https://atomgpt.org/raman .

items.title: Reconstruction of the Calligraphy Education Model in the Digital-Intelligent Transformation
items.abstract: The digital-intelligent transformation of traditional calligraphy education is advancing through the integration of artificial intelligence, big data, and immersive technologies. This study proposes a Dual Helix Reconstruction Model that synergistically couples a data chain with a teaching chain, establishing a closed-loop learning ecosystem incorporating intelligent handwriting analysis, contextual immersion, and collaborative feedback. A longitudinal experiment conducted in an authentic calligraphy course demonstrated the model's efficacy through multisource evidence. Results showed significant improvements in writing precision (d = 0.91), fluency (d = 0.85), and learning motivation (d = 0.88), confirming its role in enhancing skill acquisition, engagement, and self-regulation. Furthermore, the model fostered the integrated development of artistic expression and cultural understanding. This research provides a replicable paradigm for the digital-intelligent evolution of calligraphy education and contributes a methodological foundation for interdisciplinary innovation in art pedagogy.

items.title: Recreation Perceptions Across Access Settings in Mountainous Linear Cultural Heritage: Evidence from the Great Wall
items.abstract: Mountainous linear cultural heritage corridors include both formal-access and restricted-access sections, but recreation perceptions across these settings remain insufficiently understood. Using 17,034 online reviews from 18 Ming Great Wall sections in the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region, China, this study compared perception-element prominence, sentiment orientations, and textual co-occurrence through an integrated analytical framework, LLM-assisted labelling, statistical comparisons, section-level sensitivity analyses, and co-occurrence networks. Embodied recreation was prominent in both settings. Section-level comparisons showed greater attention to management and services, particularly entry costs and infrastructure, in formal-access sections, whereas mountain environments and risk and use impacts were more prominent in restricted-access sections, particularly naturalness and heritage preservation. Although sentiment profiles differed descriptively, no section-level sentiment comparisons remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Co-occurrence analysis revealed associations between infrastructure and embodied recreation in formal-access reviews, while restricted-access reviews linked heritage preservation, mountain environments, bodily activity, and safety concerns. By extending recreation-perception analysis beyond formally managed attractions, this study provides comparative evidence of shared recreational interests and differentiated management concerns within a continuous heritage corridor. The findings inform access-sensitive management and corridor-scale heritage conservation, subject to limitations associated with platform coverage and reviewer self-selection.

items.title: Resistance and Response as AI Literacy: What Creative-Arts Educators Can Learn from Student Resistance and Adaptation of AI
items.abstract: Today, many educational institutions are incorporating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into their curricula, although skepticism is increasing among younger generations, particularly in Australia and the United States. Some students are organizing opposition to the use of generative AI in coursework. The creative industry continues to experiment with AI-based production methods, and art museums and film festivals are featuring AI-generated works. Countries such as China maintain a highly optimistic perspective on the technology. This panel convenes experts from Australia, China, South Korea, and the United States to examine critical questions regarding the role of AI in education and the arts.

items.title: Responding Fairly: Integrating Critical Controls, Incident Investigation and Human Factors to Strengthen Organisational Learning
items.abstract: Background: High-potential incidents in construction are often initially understood through the actions of the person closest to the event. This can narrow investigations, obscure the operational and organisational conditions that shaped performance, and weaken both learning and trust. As HEB Construction’s Critical Control Management programme matured, the organisation identified a disconnect between its prevention approach and the way incidents, individual actions and accountability were considered. Aim: This practice case study describes the development and implementation of Responding Fairly, an approach intended to connect Critical Control Management, Incident Cause Analysis Method investigations, Human and Organisational Performance principles, and people processes. Its purpose is to support fair, consistent and evidence-informed decisions while maintaining accountability. Approach: Rather than introducing a separate process, HEB aligned existing investigation, critical control and people practices around a shared sequence of questions. Investigations first consider which controls should have prevented the event, whether those controls were present and effective, how the work was designed and supported, and which conditions influenced decisions at the time. Individual actions are considered after this context has been established. The approach is jointly supported by Operations, Health and Safety, and Human Resources, with leader coaching and practical guidance used to strengthen consistency. Practice example and findings: A service-strike investigation showed how an apparent failure by an operator was better understood when outdated plans, a changed work scope, conflicting site markings, unavailable technical support and time pressure were examined together. This broader analysis led to strengthened service verification requirements, revalidation following scope changes and clearer excavation controls. Early implementation experience indicates richer learning, more targeted corrective actions, greater leader confidence and improved worker perceptions of fairness. Conclusion: Responding Fairly demonstrates how prevention, investigation and accountability can be treated as one connected learning system. Context does not remove accountability; it enables accountability to be located more fairly and supported by fuller evidence. The experience also suggests that a framework alone is insufficient: leaders require capability, support and confidence to pause, tolerate uncertainty and understand the conditions surrounding an event before reaching conclusions.

items.title: Responsible AI Leadership and Employee Idea Implementation: The Mediating Role of Human–Ai Knowledge Integration in Corporate Organizations and Higher Education Institutions
items.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into organizational practices has raised important questions about responsible leadership, knowledge integration, and employee innovation. This study examined the relationship between responsible AI leadership and employee idea implementation, with human–AI knowledge integration as the mediating variable, among employees of corporate organizations and higher education institutions in Metro Manila, Philippines. A quantitative, cross-sectional, explanatory-correlational, and comparative research design was employed, involving 400 respondents equally distributed between the two organizational sectors. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire employing a four-point Likert scale and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), bootstrap mediation analysis, and multi-group SEM. The study investigated the direct relationships among the three variables, determined the mediating role of human–AI knowledge integration, and examined differences in structural relationships between the two sectors. The final findings revealed significant positive relationships among responsible AI leadership, human–AI knowledge integration, and employee idea implementation. Human–AI knowledge integration partially mediated the relationship between responsible AI leadership and employee idea implementation, while no statistically significant differences were established between the two organizational sectors. Anchored in Socio-Technical Systems Theory and the Knowledge-Based View, the study's final framework emphasizes the importance of combining ethical AI leadership practices with employees' professional knowledge and judgment. The findings demonstrate that responsible AI leadership is positively associated with employees' ability to translate AI-supported insights into practical workplace improvements. The study provides empirical evidence to guide responsible AI governance, employee capability development, knowledge-sharing initiatives, and organizational innovation strategies across corporate and higher education environments.

items.title: Responsive Cues Converted Into Reciprocal Obligation: When Something That Answers Seems to Be Owed, or to Owe
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Responsive Cues Converted Into Reciprocal Obligation, a mechanism through which repeated signs of attention can lead someone to feel that care is owed in either direction. A device that comes when called or asks to be held may come to seem like a companion who depends on its owner. The owner, in turn, may expect someone to keep that companion functioning. The mechanism concerns the point at which such an expectation extends beyond any commitment established by the people or institutions behind the device. The paper places this account alongside Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass’s work on how people apply social conventions to computers and other media. It asks what a particular person came to expect, which words or actions connect that expectation to a responsive cue, and who undertook to honor it. A person’s account of companionship can establish what the relationship meant to them. A provider’s statements and policies supply evidence about what that provider promised. Sony’s AIBO illustrates the distinction. Sony offered repairs for its earlier models for stated periods, and its repair clinic operated beyond the latest deadline in its notice. In 2018, owners of the new aibo asked Sony to extend its policy of providing repairs for seven years after withdrawal from sale. The founder of A FUN, an independent repair firm, argued that Sony bore continuing responsibility for the companion it had brought to market. The paper leaves the merits of that demand open. GROOVE X’s LOVOT provides a contrast through priced care plans whose written terms specify what the maker will cover. Part of the Presence Through Technology series within On Human Modeling, the paper also offers a way to examine expectations of discretion in human–AI interaction. A conversational assistant might recall a private concern and ask about it weeks later. If the user explains that being remembered led them to expect the exchange to stay private, that account connects a specific cue to a specific expectation. The provider’s confidentiality commitments can then be compared with what the user understood.

items.title: Rethinking audits in the age of ESG
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to systematically examine the core themes and boundaries of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) assurance, identifying prevailing research hotspots and dominant scholarly conversations. Furthermore, this study seeks to uncover emerging areas and critical gaps that offer opportunities for future research to address current and evolving challenges in ESG assurance. Design/methodology/approach Based on 148 peer-reviewed articles (after rigorous screening), the authors use bibliometric techniques, including network analysis, clustering and co-citation analysis, to synthesise the field’s evolution and reveal underexplored areas. Findings The review identifies five priority directions for future inquiry: the professionalism and evolving role of ESG assurers, ESG assurance quality and firm performance, the influence of governance mechanisms and stakeholder pressures, the implications of Audit 4.0 technologies (e.g. artificial intelligence, blockchain and data analytics) for assurance legitimacy and impact of agentic AI on assurance providers and ESG reporting readability and its consequences for assurance outcomes. By highlighting persistent tensions, contradictions and unresolved debates, this study reconceptualises ESG assurance as an evolving, multidisciplinary domain. Research limitations/implications This study may fully rely on Scopus, which limits the scope by potentially excluding relevant studies from other databases. Further, this paper addresses the key challenges found by International Federation of Accountants (IFAC, 2021), in determining the scope of an assurance engagement, exercising professional scepticism and judgment and obtaining the necessary competency and skills. Practical implications This study advances the emerging field of ESG assurance by identifying underexplored research areas, highlighting key research gaps and outlining promising directions for future inquiry. Beyond mapping the existing literature, this study also discusses the possible theoretical contributions that can strengthen the conceptual development of this domain. The review highlights key practical issues, including the role of governance, AI adoption and assurer professionalism in enhancing the credibility and transparency of ESG assurance. This study offers useful insights for researchers, practitioners, standard setters and regulators aiming to strengthen the quality and reliability of ESG assurance. Social implications This study’s insights can enhance transparency and accountability in ESG reporting, fostering trust among stakeholders such as investors and regulators. Improving ESG assurance practices encourages companies to adopt more responsible and sustainable approaches, benefiting society at large. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study is among the first multi-disciplinary systematic literature reviews to study potential future avenues in the ESG assurance area with a holistic view. This study introduces diverse significant areas to meet current challenges in ESG assurance practices.

items.title: Revocation Window in RAG: Quantifying Unauthorized Retrieval Exposure During Access-Control Propagation
items.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often store document chunks in a vector index together with a copy of their access-control metadata. When a user's permission is revoked in the authoritative permission store, this indexed copy may remain stale, allowing the vector database to keep returning protected content. This paper measures the duration of this revocation window and separates two outcomes: unauthorized index retrieval, in which the vector database returns a protected chunk, and LLM-context exposure, in which that chunk reaches the context assembled for the language model. We built a controlled synthetic testbed with PostgreSQL as the authoritative permission store and Qdrant as the vector index, and evaluated six enforcement configurations: periodic synchronization, event-driven synchronization, a no-worker control, query-time authorization, hybrid authorization, and query-time authorization with a 10-second decision cache. Each configuration retained 27 trials (5 for the control) within a 35-second observation window. The median context-level revocation propagation time was 9.92 s for 20-second periodic synchronization, 14 ms for event-driven synchronization, and 4.98 s for the cached query-time configuration. Under periodic synchronization, 87.7% of relevant queries placed the protected chunk in the context before revocation was enforced. Query-time and hybrid authorization blocked protected content at the first post-revocation probe (0 ms at probe resolution) even though the stale index kept returning it, while the no-worker control never achieved stable enforcement within the window. These findings describe the tested synthetic testbed and are not production guarantees.
